📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR -- For those of you who don't have time to read 5,000 words about async RL plumbing (we get it, you have models to train):.

If you'd rather skip straight to the good part, here's the full comparison table (no reading required, we won't judge).

But seriously, if you stick around, you might learn a thing or two about why your GPUs are idle 60% of the time.

Async RL training has emerged as the dominant paradigm for post-training at scale. Several trends in modern post-training have made synchronous training loops nearly impossible to scale:.

The open-source ecosystem has converged on a common architectural response: disaggregate inference from training onto separate GPU pools, connect them with a rollout buffer, and let both sides run concurrently.

According to recent reports, we are developing a latest async trainer for TRL, one of the most widely used libraries for model post-training. To guide our design, we surveyed sixteen open-source libraries that were built from the ground up around asynchronous training and compared them across seven axes: orchestration primitives, buffer design, weight sync protocols, staleness management, partial rollout handling, LoRA support, and distributed training backends. This article distills the design principles we extracted from that survey.

Beyond RL, the need for async infrastructure is increasingly evident. For example, on-policy distillation, where a student generates sequences and a teacher scores them, mirrors GRPO but swaps the reward function for a teacher forward pass. Recognizing this structural similarity, everything in this survey applies equally to async distillation. We'll return to this broader point in Section 5.

According to recent reports, TRL's current GRPOTrainer implements the full GRPO loop (prompt sampling, generation, reward scoring, advantage computation, gradient revision, and weight sync) in a single synchronous training_step() call. This design is simple and correct, but it cannot overlap generation with training, leaving significant GPU utilisation on the table.

Looking at the GRPOTrainer, we have the following phases sequentially within each training step:.

Each phase blocks until completion before the next begins. The timeline looks like this:.

It has been revealed that TRL offers the steps_per_generation config option to reuse a single set of rollouts across multiple gradient steps (temporal reuse), amortizing the generation cost. But the generation call itself remains fully synchronous and blocking; the trainer cannot begin gradient computation until every completion in the batch has finished.

The library also supports running vLLM in server mode as a separate process. It frees the training GPU during generation, but two hard synchronisation barriers remain: the HTTP calls until all completions return, and the weight sync blocks both the trainer and vLLM during the transfer.

Before discussing async training, it is essential to understand the two deployment topologies for RL training with a separate inference engine:.

According to recent reports, the biggest advantage of the disaggregated mode is that inference and training can run concurrently. While the trainer computes gradients on batch N, the inference pool is already generating rollouts for batch N+K, enabling async training. However, this benefit comes at a cost: additional GPUs are required.

Sources indicate that concurrency, asynchronicity, and parallelism are distinct concepts that often get conflated. In this article, when we say "async training," we mean something specific: generation and training running in parallel, with effective overlap; the inference pool is producing the next batch of rollouts while the training pool is computing gradients on the current batch. This is fundamentally a disaggregated-mode capability. Colocated mode can benefit from optimisations like sleep/wake memory management or fast in-place resharding to speed up inference, but it cannot achieve true simultaneous overlap; inference and training still take turns on the same GPUs. Every library in this survey that implements meaningful async overlap uses disaggregated mode as the foundation.

Industry observers note that in RL training for reasoning models, autoregressive generation dominates wall-clock time. A single rollout for a math or coding task can produce 8K–64K tokens of chain-of-thought reasoning (see QED-Nano rollout lengths).

To ground this concretely, consider vLLM benchmarks on a single H100 80GB GPU (bf16, no quantisation, offline throughput mode). A 7B model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) achieves ~6,300 output tokens/s aggregate throughput; a 32B model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) drops to ~1,200 output tokens/s. These are total throughput across all concurrent requests, the number the inference engine can push through per second, regardless of how many sequences share the GPU.

Sources indicate that now consider a typical GRPO training step: G=8 completions per prompt × 64 prompts/batch = 512 rollouts. How long does generation take?

Recent findings suggest that even at the short end (2K tokens generated with a 7B model), generation alone consumes several minutes per training step. At the long end, where frontier reasoning models increasingly operate, a single generation phase can take hours on one GPU. Scaling to 8 inference GPUs divides these times by roughly 8× (assuming linear throughput scaling), but even then, 32K-token rollouts on a 32B model still take ~28 minutes per step.

The straggler problem compounds this further. In group-based algorithms like GRPO, you sample G completions per prompt. The batch cannot proceed until the slowest completion finishes. Chain-of-thought output lengths are highly variable; a single prompt might produce completions ranging from 1K to 32K tokens. The batch is gated by the longest completion, and continuous batching only partially mitigates this: shorter sequences free up slots for newly introduced work, but the last sequence in a GRPO group still blocks the group's reward computation and training step.

Every library in this survey has independently converged on the same architectural principle: physically separate inference GPUs from training GPUs, and push weights asynchronously, so generation never stops and training never waits.

Industry observers note that the inference pool runs continuously, feeding completed rollouts into a buffer. The training pool pulls from the buffer, computes gradient updates, and periodically pushes upcoming weights back to the inference pool to keep it in sync. The two loops run at their own pace, decoupled by the buffer.

This setup is highly scalable, but it introduces a new class of problems: staleness (rollouts generated under an old policy), weight synchronisation overhead, partial rollout handling, etc. The rest of this article dissects in detail how current open-source libraries address these challenges.

To make sense of the rapidly expanding ecosystem of async RL libraries, we propose seven orthogonal axes of comparison. Each axis captures a fundamental design decision that shapes the library's performance, complexity, and trade-offs.

How does the system coordinate its distributed components?

The choice of orchestration framework determines the programming model, failure semantics, and scalability ceiling. Rather than listing per-library implementation details, the landscape decomposes cleanly into four orchestration types, fundamental coordination paradigms that differ in abstraction level, failure model, and deployment requirements:.

Note on Tunix: Tunix (Google) uses a JAX-native mesh model with ThreadPoolExecutor for async overlap and jax.device_put for cross-mesh weight transfer. It is architecturally distinct enough from the PyTorch ecosystem that direct comparison on orchestration is not meaningful; it lives in the XLA/TPU world with its own coordination primitives.

The table above reveals a striking pattern: eight of the sixteen libraries surveyed use Ray as their orchestration backbone. This is not a coincidence; it reflects a deep architectural fit between the actor model and the structure of RL training. A survey by Anyscale (the firm behind Ray) of open-source RL libraries for LLMs confirms this convergence. RL training at large scales involves fundamentally heterogeneous components (inference engines, training engines, environments, reward models) that must be orchestrated across a cluster, often on different hardware types, with different scaling requirements and failure modes. Ray's actor model maps directly onto this:.

Actor isolation and heterogeneous resources. Each RL component (vLLM inference server, FSDP trainer, reward model, environment pool) becomes a Ray actor with its own resource requirements (num_gpus, num_cpus, memory). Placement groups give fine-grained control over GPU affinity without manual SSH/torchrun orchestration.

According to recent reports, scheduling and autoscaling. Ray's scheduler handles the combinatorial problem of placing heterogeneous actors across a cluster. When generation requires 8× more GPU-hours than training, you can just tell Ray to scale your inference actors independently.

Fault tolerance. Long RL training runs (days to weeks) are vulnerable to GPU failures, OOM kills, and network partitions. Ray's actor restart policies and object store replication provide resilience that would require significant custom infrastructure with raw asyncio and multiprocessing. Concrete example of the fault tolerance: open-instruct, for example, relies on Ray's actor supervision to recover from vLLM engine crashes mid-rollout.

According to recent reports, object store for zero-copy data transfer. Rollout data can be large, tens of GB per batch for very long-context reasoning. Ray's shared-memory object store enables zero-copy transfer between actors on the same node, avoiding serialization overhead that usually comes with multiprocessing.Queue approaches.

Recent findings suggest that ecosystem maturity. Ray has been battle-tested at scale since 2017, with production deployments on thousands of GPUs. The debugging overhead is real (Ray Dashboard, distributed stack traces, placement group failures), but the alternative, building equivalent coordination from scratch, is worse at the multi-node scale. That mentioned, Ray is a heavy dependency: it pulls in its own scheduler, object store, and dashboard, adding operational complexity that not every team needs. This is exactly why libraries like PRIME-RL, PipelineRL, and AReaL opted for lightweight native-Python coordination (asyncio, threading, Redis streams) instead --- when you control the full stack and your deployment topology is fixed, the simplicity and debuggability of vanilla Python often outweigh the conveniences Ray provides.

The cost is a hard dependency on a non-trivial runtime. This trade-off can be worthwhile, especially for production-scale training (64+ GPUs, multi-day runs, complicated reward computation).

Recent findings suggest that while Ray's actor model is the main player on the field, Monarch emerged as a new PyTorch-native distributed actor framework from Meta, purpose-built for GPU workloads. Like Ray, Monarch is based on the actor model; components are independent actors with mailboxes communicating via messages, but it is designed from the ground up for the PyTorch/CUDA ecosystem rather than being a general-purpose distributed runtime.

Monarch offers several capabilities particularly relevant to async RL. An example implementation of async RL with Monarch (from the GPU Mode lecture series) demonstrates the architecture: generators, a replay buffer, and a trainer are modelled as Monarch actors, with the replay buffer absorbing latency variance from straggler rollouts and RDMA weight sync pushing updated parameters to generators without blocking training. The pattern is structurally identical to Ray-based designs (verl, SkyRL, open-instruct) but implemented with pure PyTorch-native primitives.

How do generated rollouts flow from inference to training, and how deep is the pipeline?

It has been revealed that the buffer is the data structure sitting between generation and training. Its depth controls the maximum degree of asynchrony, and therefore the maximum staleness.

The double-buffer pattern is the simplest upgrade from synchronous to asynchronous training: it overlaps exactly one generation with one training step and introduces at most one step of policy lag !

Deeper queues, on the other hand, improve throughput but require staleness management.

It has been revealed that the buffer controls how much data is in flight. But data is only half the equation. The other half is getting updated weights back to the inference servers before those rollouts go stale. That's where weight sync comes in!

How do new model weights reach the inference servers after a gradient enhancement?

Industry observers note that scope note: This axis focuses on disaggregated mode, where inference and training run on separate GPU pools, since that is the deployment topology where async overlap (and therefore weight sync design) actually matters. Colocated setups (same GPUs for both roles) are inherently synchronous and do not face the transport/interrupt trade-offs discussed below.

It has been revealed that this is the most architecturally consequential axis. The protocol determines sync latency, interrupt granularity, and whether partial rollouts are possible.

Sources indicate that there is a critical distinction to make here: the transport mechanism and the interrupt model. Most libraries pause generation at a coarse boundary, an HTTP request, a full batch, or even a full training step, before initiating weight transfer. PipelineRL is the outlier: it never stops generating at all.

In the interrupt model, when does the generation pause to accept newly introduced weights?

This is where PipelineRL fundamentally diverges from every other library. Rather than listing each library individually, the landscape collapses into five conceptual tiers, ordered from finest to coarsest interrupt granularity:.

The "never-stop" tier is qualitatively different from all others: PipelineRL, for example, hooks into the inference engine so that the lock is acquired and released per transformer forward pass (one token step for one sequence). A weight update waits at most one forward pass (~few ms), swaps all parameters, and generation resumes immediately. Every other library stops generation at a coarser boundary, from one HTTP request (~hundreds of ms) up to a full batch boundary (~seconds).

Weight sync controls when new weights arrive. But async training means rollouts are always being generated under some policy version, and that generating policy might be several gradient steps behind the trainer. How libraries handle this policy lag is staleness management.

How does the system handle the fact that generated rollouts may come from an older policy than the one being trained?

It has been revealed that once generation and training overlap, samples become off-policy. Three orthogonal strategies have emerged for managing this staleness, and most production systems combine more than one:.

Strategy 1: Per-sample version rejection. Every sample is tagged with the integer policy version that generated it. At training time, samples whose version falls behind the current policy by more than a threshold are hard-dropped before entering the loss computation. Simple and correct, but wastes the precious compute spent generating discarded samples.

Strategy 2, Depth Bounding. The queue or buffer between generation and training has a bounded capacity (or an explicit staleness gate), which architecturally limits how far behind any sample can be. This ranges from depth=1 (one-step-ahead double buffering, where staleness is impossible by construction) to explicit capacity formulas tied to version gaps. No per-sample version tracking is required; the bound is enforced by the system's pipeline depth.

Strategy 3, IS-weighted loss correction. Stale samples that reach the trainer are reweighted by the importance sampling ratio π∗θ(a∣s)π∗old(a∣s)\frac{\pi*{\theta}(a \mid s)}{\pi*{\text{old}}(a \mid s)}π∗old(a∣s)π∗θ(a∣s)​, typically clipped (Truncated IS). Some libraries also apply OPSM (zero-out loss for off-policy samples with negative advantage). This preserves throughput; no samples are discarded, but there is a cost in gradient variance from the IS ratios.

It has been revealed that these strategies are orthogonal: a system can use version rejection alone, depth bounding alone, IS correction alone, or any combination of them. Synchronous systems avoid the problem entirely by never overlapping generation and training.

✅ = yes, ❌ = no, ⚠️ = optional / configurable, — = not applicable (synchronous).

The trend in production systems (PRIME-RL, AReaL, open-instruct) is toward hybrid approaches that combine depth bounding with optional IS correction, getting the architectural simplicity of bounded queues with the loss-level safety net of importance weighting for stable training.

It has been revealed that staleness management handles data that was generated under an old policy. But what about data that's still being generated when a weight enhancement lands?

What happens to a generation in progress when a weight enhancement arrives?

In a recent development, this is critical for long-context tasks where a single rollout can take minutes. Four strategies:.

So far, every axis has assumed full-parameter training. But in LoRA training, you're only training a few million adapter parameters instead of billions, the weight sync problem nearly disappears. Let's look at how these libraries support LoRA training.

Does the library support parameter-efficient training via LoRA adapters, in what modes, and does it exploit adapter-only weight sync?

Sources indicate that loRA is arguably the most practically consequential axis for teams with limited GPU budgets. It reduces the trainable parameter count by 99%+, halves peak activation memory, and, when the inference server is LoRA-aware, enables adapter-only weight sync: instead of broadcasting every parameter of a 7B+ model (~100–500ms NCCL), only the adapter deltas are pushed to vLLM, which at rank 32 amounts to ~50 MB, a sub-millisecond transfer.

* NeMo-RL: LoRA for GRPO and DPO is supported only on the DTensor backend; the Megatron Core backend is SFT-only (RL LoRA listed as "coming soon"). Uses a custom DTensor-compatible LoRA module (not peft), optionally with Triton kernels.

† ROLL: LoRA is officially supported with the DeepSpeed training backend only. Megatron-backend LoRA appeared in the Feb 2026 changelog but remains experimental.

‡ open-instruct: The model config exposes LoRA-related fields (use_peft, lora_r, lora_alpha), and adapter saving is handled in the checkpoint logic. However, the peft model is never initialised in the RL training path; LoRA remains an SFT/DPO-only feature for the RL trainer as of March 2026.

Three LoRA implementation families:.

According to recent reports, huggingFace peft (PipelineRL, SkyRL/FSDP, verifiers-rl, ROLL, OAT, Atropos): The most common choice. Standard checkpoint format (adapter_model.safetensors), compatible with any HF Transformers training loop. ZeRO-3 interactions require care: OAT, for example, needs to disable the fused LM head; ROLL must disable gradient checkpointing entirely.

Sources indicate that megatron-Bridge (verl/Megatron, SkyRL/Megatron, MILES): Required for 3D-parallel training (TP × PP × DP). Supports multiple LoRA types: lora, canonical_lora (splits merged QKV → separate Q/K/V adapters), vlm_lora, and dora. The canonical_lora variant avoids the QKV merge, thereby improving training stability. MILES saves checkpoints in both HF peft format and Megatron-native per-rank format.

Sources indicate that custom implementations (NeMo-RL, PRIME-RL, Tunix/qwix): Library-specific LoRA modules not interoperable with peft checkpoints. PRIME-RL uniquely supports multiple simultaneous adapters in a single run for multi-experiment parallelism. Tunix uses Google's qwix JAX library, which adds built-in QLoRA (NF4 quantization) and TPU-native gradient routing. NeMo-RL uses a custom DTensor-compatible module with an optional Triton fused kernel.

The adapter-only weight sync opportunity (interaction with Axis 3):.

It has been revealed that eight of the thirteen libraries support pushing only the LoRA adapter deltas to the inference server. This changes the character of the weight sync problem (Axis 3) entirely. When using full-parameter training, the interrupt model (per-forward-pass lock vs. per-request abort vs. per-batch pause) determines how much generation is wasted during an NCCL broadcast. When using LoRA with adapter-only sync, the transfer is so small that nearly any interrupt model delivers equivalent throughput! Even Atropos's brute-force HTTP hot-swap becomes viable.

What parallelism strategy does the library use for training, and how does this constrain or enable the async architecture?

This axis cuts across every other axis. The choice of training backend determines how large a model can fit per GPU, how many collective operations are needed to gather weights before broadcasting to inference servers, and which model architectures can be trained at all. It is the single most consequential decision for teams scaling beyond 30B parameters or moving from dense to Mixture-of-Experts models.

The training backend creates direct implications for async RL library design:.

Weight sync speed is a direct function of the training backend, and faster sync means less staleness.

In a disaggregated async setup, weight sync does not necessarily stall inference. The key design decision is how the weight upgrade interacts with in-flight generation; four strategies exist, ordered from least to most disruptive:.

But even in libraries where inference continues, slower sync means longer periods where inference runs on stale weights. The policy version gap between the trainer and the inference pool grows with sync duration. Something to take into account.

Industry observers note that **MoE support is an increasingly important differentiator as the field moves toward sparse models.**The trend is clear: frontier models are sparse (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-MoE, Mixtral, DBRX), and open-weight MoEs are becoming the default starting point for post-training. Training these models requires Expert Parallelism (EP), distributing different experts to different ranks, which most async RL libraries do not support. Only Megatron-backed libraries (verl, SLIME, MILES, ROLL, NeMo-RL) and PRIME-RL's FSDP2+EP path handle EP correctly. ZeRO-based libraries (PipelineRL, verifiers-rl, OAT, open-instruct) can load MoE HuggingFace model classes, but without EP each expert is sharded across all ZeRO-3 ranks rather than being placed on a dedicated rank; every forward pass AllGathers every expert, negating the sparsity advantage entirely. EP also complicates weight sync: before broadcasting to vLLM/SGLang (which typically serves all experts from a single TP group), the trainer must AllGather expert parameters from every EP rank, an O(N∗experts×E∗size) O(N*{\text{experts}} \times E*{\text{size}}) O(N∗experts×E∗size) communication (where E_size E\_{\text{size}} E_size is the parameter count per expert) that does not exist for dense models. For a 235B MoE with 256 experts, this is a substantial sync cost. Libraries that want to remain relevant for post-training on the next generation of open MoE models need EP-aware training *and* EP-aware weight sync.

It has been revealed that **MoE LoRA is an emerging requirement, and a tricky one.**LoRA on dense models is well-understood (Axis 6): attach adapters to attention projections, train them, sync only the adapter deltas. MoE LoRA is harder because the natural target is the expert FFN layers, meaning each expert gets its own adapter. For a model with 64 experts and rank-32 LoRA on each expert's gate/up/down projections, the adapter count jumps from ~20 (dense) to ~200+ (MoE), and the adapters are distributed across EP ranks. Weight sync must gather adapters from every EP rank before pushing them to the inference server, a coordination problem that does not exist for dense LoRA. On the training side, ART explicitly implements MoE expert LoRA layers (Megatron EP path with per-expert LoRA and manual allreduce), MILES supports LoRA via Megatron-Bridge which can target expert layers, and PRIME-RL also supports MoE LoRA via a custom MultiMoELoRA module. verl's Megatron-Bridge path supports LoRA types including vlm_lora, but MoE-specific expert LoRA is not documented. On the inference side, vLLM has supported per-expert LoRA loading and serving for MoEs via fused Triton kernels for several releases, while SGLang has an open PR to add MoE LoRA support. Support for expert parallel inference with MoE LoRAs is currently in the works for both vLLM and SGLang. As MoE models become the default for post-training, MoE LoRA with efficient adapter-only sync will be a key capability gap to close.

It has been revealed that that covers the seven axes, each captures a different facet of the same underlying problem. Together, they give us a complete lens for comparing libraries. Time to put it all on one page.

Industry observers note that note: This overview reflects the state of these libraries as of March 2026. The ecosystem is evolving rapidly; specific features, backends, and integrations may change in the near future.

That's the current state of play. But the field is moving fast, and several emerging trends are about to stress-test these architectures in ways their designers may not have anticipated.

Recent findings suggest that the trends below are not a catalogue of new techniques; each one creates concrete pressure on the infrastructure and algorithmic choices made today. The question is not "what is the frontier?" but "if this trend wins, what breaks in my current stack?".

Sources indicate that PPO's value network doubles the memory footprint of any training node. The field is converging on critic-free variants (GRPO, REINFORCE++, Online DPO) precisely because long CoT reasoning makes this overhead prohibitive at 8K–64K context lengths.

What this unlocks: Eliminating the critic frees ~50% of training GPU memory. This slack can be reallocated to: (a) larger rollout batches, directly reducing the straggler variance problem, or (b) co-locating inference and training on the same GPUs, which eliminates the need for a separate NCCL weight sync process group entirely.

It has been revealed that what it does not solve: Critic-free methods still require frequent weight pushes to inference servers. In fact, they can increase sync pressure: without a value network to provide a stable baseline, GRPO-style algorithms require larger group sizes (G=8–32) to get low-variance advantage estimates, which means more rollouts per step and faster policy drift. Libraries that sync only at coarse boundaries (per training step or per K steps) will see staleness grow faster under critic-free training.

Asymmetric trajectory filtering (GRPO-RoC: oversample rollouts, strictly filter positives, uniformly downsample negatives; CISPO/DAPO-style asymmetric clipping in DeepSeek-V3.2 and MiniMax-M1) has a subtler impact on staleness. The concern is not the batch shrinking per se; it is the composition of the surviving batch. Positive trajectories (correct solutions to easy prompts) converge faster and are retained preferentially; harder prompts yield mostly negative trajectories that are discarded. The result: the samples that survive filtering are systematically older than the average rollout in the buffer, because the easy prompts they solve were issued earlier in training. A buffer full of nominally "fresh" rollouts can contain surviving positives spanning a wide range of policy versions. Admission control that tracks staleness at the batch level (e.g., SkyRL's max_staleness_steps capacity gate, Atropos's max_batches_offpolicy) cannot detect this intra-batch version spread. Per-sample version tagging (Axis 4) is not optional in this regime; the trainer must be able to reject or IS-correct individual samples whose policy version diverges too far, even if the batch they belong to was admitted recently.

Critic-free methods simplify the training side. But the scoring side is about to get more expensive: process reward models score intermediate reasoning steps, not just final answers, and that introduces a whole latest synchronisation bottleneck.

Industry observers note that outcome reward is scalar and cheap, one call to a verifier at the end of a rollout. Process reward models (PRMs) score intermediate steps, which require either (a) a separate PRM forward pass over the full reasoning trace, or (b) an online utility function computed token-by-token during generation.

Industry observers note that PRPO (entropy-spike segmentation with PRM scoring per segment) and DEEP-GRPO (pivot identification via online utility) both incur computational overhead between generation and training. In the current library landscape, this phase maps awkwardly onto the preprocessor pool (PipelineRL) or requires an additional Ray actor (verl, NeMo-RL). Neither is designed for it.

The key implication: PRM-based credit assignment breaks the assumption that rewards are cheap to compute. A PRM forward pass over a 32K-token reasoning trace from a 7B model can be very costly. At G=8 completions per prompt, the reward computation could consume non-negligible wall time relative to the generation itself. Two consequences:.

It has been revealed that DEEP-GRPO's pivot resampling introduces a third-generation pattern alongside standard rollouts and partial rollout resumes: local resampling from a mid-sequence state. This requires saving KV cache state at pivot points, which no current async library supports out of the box. Weight sync at pivot boundaries could be a latest correctness requirement: if weights change between the pivot generation and the local resample, the advantage estimate is corrupted. We can, of course, recompute the KV-cache in a single prefill, but it could waste precious compute in our training.

Sources indicate that single-agent GRPO trains one policy generating G completions per prompt. Emerging, multi-agent self-play means the effective "group" spans multiple model invocations sequentially chained. The reward is only available after all models in the chain are complete.

Straggler dynamics change qualitatively. In single-agent GRPO, the straggler is the longest completion in a group, a tail event in a unimodal length distribution. In multi-agent pipelines, the straggler is the product of two or more length distributions. In a Proposer/Solver multi-agent architecture, if each has a 90th percentile completion time (5× the median), the joint 90th percentile is roughly 25× the median.

RL on swarms of agents implies a new unit of work. Today, the atomic unit in every library is a single (prompt, completion, reward) triple. In multi-agent training, the atomic unit becomes an episode, a directed graph of turns, tool calls, and inter-agent messages. Buffer design, staleness tracking, and advantage computation all need to operate over episodes. Replaying or forking episodes could also be necessary.

Recent findings suggest that straggler problems across agents are bad enough when the model is at least internally consistent. With MoE architectures, even a single model can disagree with itself across inference and training frameworks and this raises a fresh set of emerging problems in RL training.

The training-inference mismatch problem is endemic in async RL; anytime rollout data is generated under policy π∗old\pi*{\text{old}}π∗old and gradient updates are computed under π∗θ\pi*{\theta}π∗θ, the two policies diverge. Most libraries address this with IS correction or hard version rejection. But DeepSeek-V3.2's production experience reveals two structural sources of mismatch that IS correction cannot fix.

Industry observers note that source 1: MoE expert routing inconsistency. Mixture-of-Experts models activate a sparse subset of experts per token. Inference frameworks (vLLM, SGLang) and training frameworks (Megatron, FSDP) implement the router independently, and differences in floating-point rounding in the gating function can lead to different expert selections for identical inputs. When expert routing diverges, the active parameter subspace shifts discontinuously; a gradient step computed assuming Expert A was active is applied to weights that are active under Expert B. DeepSeek-V3.2 found this "induces abrupt shifts in the active parameter subspace, which destabilizes optimization and exacerbates off-policy problems.".

It has been revealed that their solution, Keep Routing, preserves the exact expert routing paths used during sampling (inference) and enforces those paths during the training forward pass. This requires the inference framework to record and return routing decisions alongside token logprobs, and the training framework to accept and enforce them. No current open-source async RL library implements this. For any team training MoE models (DeepSeek-V3 class, Mixtral, future open MoEs), this is a correctness issue, not a performance issue.

Sources indicate that source 2: Sampling truncation mask mismatch. Top-p and top-k sampling truncate the vocabulary at generation time, excluding low-probability tokens from the sampling distribution. During training, the full vocabulary is visible to π∗θ\pi*{\theta}π∗θ. This violates the importance sampling identity: the action spaces of π∗old\pi*{\text{old}}π∗old (truncated) and π∗θ\pi*{\theta}π∗θ (full) differ, so the IS ratio π∗θ(o∗t)/π∗old(ot)\pi*{\theta}(o*t) / \pi*{\text{old}}(o_t)π∗θ(o∗t)/π∗old(ot​) is undefined for tokens that were masked during sampling.

DeepSeek-V3.2's Keep Sampling Mask solution: record the truncation mask during sampling and apply it to π_θ\pi\_{\theta}π_θ during the training forward pass, so both policies operate over the same vocabulary subset. This requires passing the mask back from the inference server to the trainer, which is again something no current library infrastructure supports.

Implications for library design: Both Keep Routing and Keep Sampling Mask require the inference server to return additional metadata alongside token logprobs, routing decisions, and sampling masks. The current API contract between inference servers (vLLM, SGLang) and trainers is (token_ids, logprobs, finish_reason). Extending this to (token_ids, logprobs, finish_reason, expert_routing, sampling_mask) is a breaking change to every library's data flow.

On-policy distillation, where a student model generates sequences, and a teacher model scores them with token-level logprobs, is structurally the same as the async coordination problem in GRPO.

Sources indicate that every design axis in this survey, rollout buffers, weight sync protocols, staleness management, and partial rollout handling, applies identically to distillation. The generation pool produces student rollouts, the teacher scores them (replacing the verifier), and the trainer computes a backward pass with either an advantage-modified GRPO loss or a standalone KL objective. Self-distillation adds one more coordination requirement: the teacher is a frozen snapshot of the student from step N−k, so the system must periodically checkpoint the policy and hot-swap the teacher server without disrupting the pipeline, a primitive that no library has fully automated.

According to recent reports, the practical implication for library design is that async RL infrastructure should not be built as a GRPO-specific system. The generation--scoring--training pipeline is a general pattern that covers RL with outcome rewards, RL with process rewards, on-policy distillation, and self-distillation. Libraries like SLIME, MILES, PRIME-RL, AReaL, and NeMo-RL already support both GRPO and on-policy distillation precisely because their async scaffolding treats the reward/scoring phase as a pluggable component rather than a hardcoded verifier call. Any async trainer that aspires to generality should do the same: define the scoring phase as an interface (an HTTP endpoint, a Ray actor, or a co-located forward pass), and let the buffer, staleness, and weight-sync machinery operate identically regardless of what fills it.

Having surveyed the full landscape, orchestration models, buffer designs, weight sync protocols, staleness strategies, and partial rollout handling, we can now lay out concrete design choices for an async trainer in TRL, along with the future-proof directions we intend to explore.

Industry observers note that one of the strengths of the current TRL implementation is that it does not depend on a heavy orchestrator system to manage the training lifecycle. Data inside the library remains native Python objects without external-library coloring. We want to preserve this: orchestration should stay as simple as possible, with no dependency on heavyweight external frameworks.

Rather than starting with double-buffering and graduating to something more granular, we go straight to a bounded queue where every token is tagged with the model_version that produced it. This is the lowest possible granularity from the start; it enables importance-sampling correction at the token level, supports simple admission gating (drop or down-weight tokens beyond a staleness threshold), and avoids the architectural debt of retrofitting token-level provenance onto a batch-level buffer later.

NCCL process groups are a necessity, and we already use them. Adding bucketing should be the next step as vLLM's NCCLWeightTransferEngine with packed=True directly supports bucketed broadcast: it packs parameters into configurable-size uint8 buffers (default 1 GB, double-buffered across CUDA streams) and broadcasts them via a dedicated NCCL communicator separate from the training process group. This eliminates the per-parameter call overhead that dominates naive broadcast, yielding a massive sync speedup.

Beyond vLLM's built-in engine, we will explore high-performance weight packing libraries for more demanding scenarios:.

Awex (inclusionAI), a dedicated weight synchronization framework for RL training that handles the hard problem of cross-engine transfer: training engines (Megatron, DeepSpeed) and inference engines (SGLang, vLLM) use completely different parallelism strategies and tensor layouts. Awex abstracts this behind a unified conversion layer and deterministic P2P transfer plans. It supports both separated-GPU and co-located (CUDA IPC) modes.

Sources indicate that mooncake Transfer Engine, SGLang has moved toward integrating the Mooncake Transfer Engine as its high-performance transport layer, with integrations spanning PD disaggregation, hierarchical KV caching, and elastic expert parallelism. For weight sync specifically, the companion checkpoint-engine project uses Mooncake's RDMA-backed P2P transfers to enhancement trillion-parameter models (Kimi-K2, 256×H20 GPUs) in ~16–17 seconds. Mooncake is now part of the PyTorch Ecosystem and also serves as a backend plugin for NVIDIA's NIXL transfer library.

Recent findings suggest that multi-turn tool-use tasks in complex environments can take minutes per rollout. Without a mechanism to handle in-flight rollouts during weight updates, sync windows become pipeline stalls. We will probably explore two strategies experimentally:.

That's the map, stay tuned, we are working on a concrete async GRPO trainer in TRL, and we'll announce it shortly 🧑‍🍳!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The PROLED MacBook Pro’s logo is lit with boring white LEDs. Missed opportunity.

According to recent reports, the PROLED MacBook Pro’s logo is lit with boring white LEDs. Missed opportunity.

Industry observers note that when Apple CEO John Ternus announced the first touchscreen Mac last month, the biggest reaction in the room wasn’t for the PROLED MacBook Pro’s OLED touchscreen or the thinner and lighter chassis; it was for the illuminated lid logo. It’s a throwback to the light-up logos on the old MacBooks, which Apple started phasing out in 2015, and which were completely gone by the 2018 MacBook Air redesign. It’s a nostalgia play, but boy did it work. It’s fun!

Industry observers note that just like in the old days, the new logo’s brightness is linked to the screen’s: The brighter or dimmer the screen, the brighter or dimmer the logo. But the light-up logo on the old MacBooks was illuminated by the screen’s backlight, and an OLED display doesn’t have one. Thanks to iFixit, we now know it’s lit by four white LEDs and synced with the screen’s brightness by software. But that means Apple could have used RGB LEDs.

Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, or anything in between? On the lid of your fresh MacBook Pro? Why not? After all, Apple insists it’s still serious about gaming, and nothing says “serious about gaming” like RGB lighting.

I was secretly hoping owners would be able to customize the illuminated lid cutout much like the Xbox logo on Microsoft’s Elite Series 2 controllers. But alas, no luck. You can turn off the illumination with some Terminal commands or take control of it with a third-party app. But when it’s lit, it’s only lit with white light. And iFixit’s teardown also showed the difficulty of accessing those LEDs (the screen delaminated and broke in the process). So we’re unlikely to see LED RGB mods for it unless someone’s brave enough to void their warranty and risk a pricey screen repair on their $3,000 laptop.

Sources indicate that the most fun you can have with the Apple lid logo is to install a free third-party app like LogoLight and have it pulse, breathe, match the beat of any music you’re playing, or flash some Morse code. There’s some fun there, but if you combined these features with a splash of color we’d really be cooking.

MacBooks aren’t gaming laptops, so RGB lighting may seem like a mismatch, but multicolor LEDs could have been a cool Easter egg. Nobody thought Apple would put a touchscreen on a MacBook either, and the iPhone Duo and HomeView also show Apple is in a newly introduced age of experimentation during the early Ternus era. Maybe if the light-up lid logo ever comes to future MacBook Airs or a MacBook Neo, Apple could cut loose a little.

  • Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage.
  • According to recent reports, the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running.
  • It has been revealed that this is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck. German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation.

According to recent reports, the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024, which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the issue wasn’t caught earlier.

It has been revealed that this is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still.

Aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few big tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.

Breaking: What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
  • A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

Industry observers note that model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

The idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below shows a typical AI model routing architecture.

According to recent reports, model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-plan people go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

It has been revealed that intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Sources indicate that two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

It has been revealed that the significant platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google claims Gemini Notebook uses its new Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

Industry observers note that cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

Industry observers note that A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

Sources indicate that fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

Industry observers note that we'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

In a recent development, the test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

According to recent reports, put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

Create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

Industry observers note that confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

Recent findings suggest that the second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

Sources indicate that if Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

According to recent reports, model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

According to recent reports, speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

Sources indicate that A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

According to recent reports, then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

In a recent development, the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

Recent findings suggest that the loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

Recent findings suggest that to optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

Recent findings suggest that the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

Industry observers note that several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

According to recent reports, hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

Recent findings suggest that an LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Sources indicate that smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

The ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

OpenRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

In a recent development, openClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

Sources indicate that an AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

In a recent development, mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

Introducing Storage Buckets on the Hugging Face Hub

📅 10 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hugging Face Models and Datasets repos are great for publishing final artifacts.
  • Storage Buckets are built exactly for this: mutable, S3-like object storage you can browse on the Hub, script from Python, or manage with the hf CLI.
  • Git starts to feel like the wrong abstraction pretty quickly when you're dealing with:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hugging Face Models and Datasets repos are great for publishing final artifacts. But production ML generates a constant stream of intermediate files (checkpoints, optimizer states, processed shards, logs, traces, etc.) that change often, arrive from many jobs at once, and rarely need version control.

Storage Buckets are built exactly for this: mutable, S3-like object storage you can browse on the Hub, script from Python, or manage with the hf CLI. And because they are backed by Xet, they are especially efficient for ML artifacts that share content across files.

Git starts to feel like the wrong abstraction pretty quickly when you're dealing with:.

The storage need in all these cases is the same: write fast, overwrite when needed, sync directories, remove stale files, and keep things moving.

It has been revealed that A Bucket is a non-versioned storage container on the Hub. It lives under a user or organization namespace, has standard Hugging Face permissions, can be private or public, has a page you can open in your browser, and can be addressed programmatically with a handle like hf://buckets/username/my-training-bucket.

Buckets are built on Xet, Hugging Face’s chunk-based storage backend, and this matters more than it might seem.

According to recent reports, instead of treating files as monolithic blobs, Xet breaks content into chunks and deduplicates across them. Upload a processed dataset that’s mostly similar to the raw one? Many chunks already exist. Store successive checkpoints where large parts of the model are frozen? Same story. Buckets skip the bytes that are already there, which means less bandwidth, faster transfers, and more efficient storage.

This is a natural fit for ML workloads. Training pipelines constantly produce families of related artifacts — raw and processed data, successive checkpoints, Agent traces and derived summaries — and Xet is designed to take advantage of that overlap.

In a recent development, for Enterprise customers, billing is based on deduplicated storage, so shared chunks directly reduce the billed footprint. Deduplication helps with both speed and cost.

Sources indicate that buckets live on the Hub, which means global storage by default. But not every workload can afford to pull data from wherever it happens to live, for distributed training and large-scale pipelines, storage location directly affects throughput.

Industry observers note that pre-warming lets you bring hot data closer to the cloud provider and region where your compute runs. Instead of data traveling across regions on every read, you declare where you need it and Buckets make sure it's already there when your jobs start. This is especially useful for training clusters that need fast access to large datasets or checkpoints, and for multi-region setups where different parts of a pipeline run in different clouds.

We are partnering with AWS and GCP to start with, more more cloud providers coming in the future.

Create a bucket for your project:.

Say your training job is writing checkpoints locally to ./checkpoints. Sync that directory into the Bucket:.

For large transfers, you might want to see what will happen before anything moves. --dry-run prints the proposal without executing anything:.

You can also save the blueprint to a file for review and apply it later:.

Once done, inspect the Bucket from the CLI:.

or browse it directly on the Hub at https://huggingface.co/buckets/username/my-training-bucket.

Sources indicate that that is the whole loop. Create a bucket, sync your working data into it, check on it when you need to, and save the versioned repo for when something is worth publishing. For one-off operations, hf buckets cp copies individual files and hf buckets remove cleans up stale objects.

Recent findings suggest that everything above also works from Python via huggingface_hub (available since v1.5.0). The API follows the same pattern: create, sync, inspect.

Recent findings suggest that this makes it straightforward to integrate Buckets into training scripts, data pipelines, or any service that manages artifacts programmatically. The Python client also supports batch uploads, selective downloads, deletes, and bucket moves for when you need finer control.

Bucket support is also available in JavaScript via @huggingface/hub (since v2.10.5), so you can integrate Buckets into Node.js services and web applications as well.

Recent findings suggest that buckets also work through HfFileSystem, the fsspec-compatible filesystem in huggingface_hub. This means you can list, read, write, and glob Bucket contents using standard filesystem operations — and any library that supports fsspec can access Buckets directly.

Because fsspec is the standard Python interface for remote filesystems, libraries like pandas, Polars, and Dask can read from and write to Buckets using hf:// paths with no extra setup:.

This makes it easy to plug Buckets into existing data workflows without changing how your code reads or writes files.

It has been revealed that buckets are the fast, mutable place where artifacts live while they are still in motion. Once something becomes a stable deliverable, it usually belongs to a versioned model or dataset repo.

On the roadmap, we blueprint to support direct transfers between Buckets and repos in both directions: promote final checkpoint weights into a model repo, or commit processed shards into a dataset repo once a pipeline completes. The working layer and the publishing layer stay separate, but fit into one continuous Hub-native workflow.

Before opening Buckets to everyone, we ran a private beta with a small group of launch partners.

A huge thank you to Jasper, Arcee, IBM, and PixAI for testing early versions, surfacing bugs, and sharing feedback that directly shaped this feature.

Recent findings suggest that storage Buckets bring a missing storage layer to the Hub. They give you a Hub-native place for the mutable, high-throughput side of ML: checkpoints, processed data, Agent traces, logs, and everything else that is useful before it becomes final.

Sources indicate that because they are built on Xet, Buckets are not just easier to use than forcing everything through Git. They are also more efficient for the kinds of related artifacts AI systems produce all the time. That means faster transfers, better deduplication, and on Enterprise aims, billing that benefits from the deduplicated footprint.

According to recent reports, if you already use the Hub, Buckets let you keep more of your workflow in one place. If you come from S3-style storage, they give you a familiar model with better alignment to AI artifacts and a clear path toward final publication on the Hub.

Buckets are included in existing Hub storage plans. Free accounts come with storage to get started, and PRO and Enterprise plans offer higher limits. See the storage page for details.

Has there been any consideration of a cold-storage tier?

There are likely users (myself included) with data that:.

Recent findings suggest that I understand that Xet and the newer storage limits reductions focus heavily on reducing your opex costs because there was a lot of abuse re: users hosting video files and uploading bogus. However, some legitmate workloads involve large static assets that are rarely accessed but still useful to keep hosted (natural disaster/fire reasons 😅).

I’m curious whether something like a lower-cost (and much slower) archival tier might eventually make sense for these cases?

We've discussed such feature internally and we might offer it at some point, but it's not in our short-term roadmap.

For now the main goal is to fuel data-heavy AI workflows 🤗.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Larger hands may struggle with the Atom Plus, but it squeezes a lot of functionality into an extremely tiny controller.

Larger hands may struggle with the Atom Plus, but it squeezes a lot of functionality into an extremely tiny controller.

Recent findings suggest that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s upcoming Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle.

According to recent reports, measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app.

Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these vital pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.).

Recent findings suggest that I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly proposal to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel.

While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction.

Recent findings suggest that the shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons.

In a recent development, I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut.

Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, upcoming ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market.

I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently unveiled Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.

After years of development, Google is launching its second foray into smart glasses with Intelligent Eyewear that supports Android and iOS. Pre-orders start today at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with the audio glasses shipping on December 10.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.

In a recent development, intelligent Eyewear is meant to be worn all day rather than the sunglasses-heavy approach taken by others. The frames are 40-44 grams with the weight balanced evenly.

Sources indicate that there is a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera for photos and videos (3K 30FPS or 1080p). You get image stabilization and HDR processing, while four microphones work to provide spatial audio capture. Google is also quite proud of its noise cancellation work.

There are two open-ear speakers for balanced audio and clear vocals. Control is done by a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes, or via voice commands, with Google debuting a newly introduced “Hey Gemini” hotword.

Another way to control Intelligent Eyewear is through your Pixel Watch or Galaxy Watch, with Fitbit Air support coming next year:.

Each pair features a physical on/off switch so you can “wear them as regular glasses only.” On the privacy front, there is a white indicator light when you take a photo or video that gets saved to your gallery. If the light is covered or maliciously disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Google running a hardware check when they are charging. Recording also stops when you take off the glasses.

Industry observers note that notably, Gemini commands that invoke the camera — like visual search or translation — will not save images or videos to your Gemini History. These visuals won’t be used to train AI models or for ad targeting. Additionally, the glasses will “automatically redact bystanders’ faces from these visuals before Gemini processes them.”.

Industry observers note that battery life (245mAh) is rated at nine hours on a single charge, with a fully topped-up charging case (Gentle Monster’s shown below) offering seven full charges. Power is transferred via contact pins located on the underside of the nose bridge.

Recent findings suggest that android XR runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. Other specifications include Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 6E, and IPX4 water resistance. Samsung is responsible for engineering the hardware, while there are two eyewear brands at launch.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three styles and a total of 14 variations. Alden, Reid, and Wren are inspired by the brand’s “most beloved silhouettes.” Pricing starts at $395 for optical and sun styles in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black.

The Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear collection features six frames in bold colors like dark red, pink, gray, and yellow, with 16 total variations. They can be paired with tinted, clear, blue, or brown lenses, with prescription options available for most designs. Pricing starts at $449 and will be available in the US and South Korea.

Intelligent Eyewear can be used for contextual visual searches, asking Gemini about your day, and having it accomplish tasks.

Google Maps offers turn-by-turn directions, while there’s real-time Google Translate in over 70 languages.

Like on phones, Gemini Guided Vision “offers conversational audio descriptions to people with vision impairments.” This can be used to read fine print, identify color differences, find items, and explore unfamiliar places.

These glasses also serve as always-available headphones with support for YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, and Audible. The Glasses companion app supports:.

Pre-orders for Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear start today with retail availability on December 10.
