Falcon Perception

📅 01 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts.
  • We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.
  • This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts. The model processes image patches + text in one sequence using a hybrid attention mask, and produces variable numbers of instances with a small, structured token interface and lightweight output heads. On SA-Co, Falcon Perception reaches 68.0 Macro-F1 (vs. 62.3 for SAM 3) with the main remaining gap being presence calibration (MCC 0.64 vs. 0.82). We also introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that breaks down performance by capability (attributes, OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relations) and by dense long-context crowded scenes.

We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.

This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.

Many open-vocabulary perception systems are built as modular pipelines: a (often frozen) vision backbone extracts features, a separate fusion/decoder stage combines them with language, and additional components handle matching and post-processing. This family of designs works well in many settings, but it comes with trade-offs: it can be hard to scale cleanly, hard to attribute improvements to the right component, and easy to accumulate complexity as we add a newly introduced fix for each failure mode.

We asked a simpler question: can a single early-fusion Transformer backbone handle both perception and language modeling, if we choose the right attention pattern, output interface, and training signal?

Recent findings suggest that in our experiments, the answer is largely yes. The rest of this post describes the main design choices and the evidence behind them.

A single autoregressive Transformer processes a unified sequence of image patches, text, and task tokens. The model predicts object properties in a fixed order: → → . Bounding box coordinates and sizes are decoded via specialized heads and re-injected as Fourier features. High-resolution segmentation masks are generated by a dot product between the token and upsampled image features.

Recent findings suggest that at its core, Falcon Perception is a dense Transformer that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space from the first layer. Instead of a separate vision backbone followed by a late-fusion decoder, we keep a single backbone and rely on masking and a lightweight output interface to make the dense prediction problem tractable.

It has been revealed that images and text have different structure: pixels are 2D and benefit from bidirectional context, while the prediction interface is naturally sequential. We address this with a hybrid attention mask:.

This allows the same backbone to behave like a bidirectional visual encoder on image tokens, while still supporting autoregressive prediction over task tokens.

Dense perception is not a fixed-size prediction problem: an image may contain zero instances or hundreds. Autoregressive generation gives a clean variable-length interface, but fully autoregressive dense generation (e.g., polygons or high-resolution masks token-by-token) quickly becomes expensive.

We use a small structured interface, Chain-of-Perception, which decomposes each instance into three steps:.

This ordering is deliberate. Committing to geometry first reduces ambiguity (“which instance?”), and makes the mask prediction step closer to pixel refinement conditioned on the resolved object.

The backbone is shared, while decoding uses lightweight heads tailored to the output type:.

Recent findings suggest that coordinate & Size Heads use Fourier feature encoding : mapping continuous coordinates through a random Gaussian projection into a high-dimensional sinusoidal space. This overcomes the spectral bias of neural networks, yielding more precise localization than discrete binning alone. Decoded coordinates are re-injected into the sequence as conditioning for subsequent tokens.

Segmentation Head computes a dot product between the token’s hidden state and content-aware upsampled image features. Because the token is produced after geometry and has access to early-fused visual context, we can avoid the separate mask-query machinery and Hungarian matching that often appears in decoder-based instance segmentation training.

According to recent reports, existing referring-expression benchmarks like RefCOCO are saturated — models routinely hit 90%+ — and they conflate what went wrong. Did the model fail because it can't read text? Can't understand spatial relationships? Can't handle a crowd?

We introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates samples by the dominant capability required:.

Each sample targets one dominant capability: OCR prompts avoid spatial qualifiers, and spatial prompts avoid in-image text disambiguators. This yields a capability profile rather than a single opaque score, and makes it easier to decide where to invest next (data, training curriculum, or post-training).

It has been revealed that rather than training from random weights (which in our ablations was unstable for segmentation), Falcon Perception initializes via multi-teacher distillation. Two strong vision teachers contribute complementary signals:.

The distilled initialization achieves 74.25% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k and 85.11% linear-probe mIoU on Pascal VOC, providing a strong visual foundation before perception-specific training.

We build the training set through a multi-stage pipeline:.

Sources indicate that we maintain a strict 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples. This makes presence calibration a first-class target: the model should reliably say “absent,” not only draw masks when confident.

Stage 1 — In-Context Listing (450 GT): The model learns to autoregressively list scene inventories — predicting text expressions and their locations. Full causal attention between queries enables learning of object co-occurrence ("fork, then knife, then plate"). This builds broad scene understanding.

Recent findings suggest that stage 2 — Task Alignment (225 GT): The attention mask is modified so queries can no longer see each other, simulating independent queries at inference time. Loss on text tokens is masked, focusing gradient signal entirely on presence classification and localization. This stage transitions from "scene understanding" to "answer this specific question.".

Recent findings suggest that stage 3 — Long-Context Finetuning (10 GT): A short phase with the mask limit raised to 600 per expression and a minimal constant learning rate. This adapts the model for extreme crowd density without forgetting earlier capabilities.

Key design choices validated through ablations:.

On the SA-Co open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark, Falcon Perception (0.6B parameters) achieves 68.0 Macro-F1, compared to 62.3 for SAM 3, with large gains on attribute-heavy (+8.2), food & drink (+12.2), and sports equipment (+4.0) splits. At the same time, Falcon Perception lags SAM 3 on presence calibration (MCC: 0.64 vs 0.82), which is the clearest remaining improvement axis.

Here's an example output — the prompt "Falcon" produces precise instance masks:.

Falcon Perception also performs well for reffering expressions, able to correctly segment the burger with a black bun in each frame of the video:.

This is where the early-fusion design highlights the largest differences:.

On simple objects, the gap is modest. As prompts become more compositional—requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, or relational binding—the gap widens.

In our PBench Dense split, Falcon Perception (0.6B) substantially outperforms generalist VLM baselines (e.g., 72.6 vs 8.9 for Qwen3-VL-30B in our evaluation setup), and matches or exceeds the 8B model on spatial and relational tiers.

As prompts grow more compositional — requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relational binding, or scaling to hundreds of instances — the early-fusion advantage becomes visually clear:.

According to recent reports, "168 wine bottles": Falcon Perception identifies the bottles labeled "168", while SAM 3 highlights every bottle. "Honolulu direction sign": Falcon reads the text to find the right sign.

"Lower meat skewer on left grill," "black car to the right of red car at bottom," "Belgian flag on the left" — Falcon Perception resolves the correct instance from spatial constraints. SAM 3 predicts false positives for multiple candidates.

According to recent reports, "Pastry next to brown round bread," "person using phone," "person holding helmet in hand" — Falcon Perception identifies the interacting instance. SAM 3 highlights all instances of the object class, ignoring the relational constraint.

"Snow goose," "pigeon," "colorful canned drinks" — Falcon Perception autoregressively segments hundreds of instances. SAM 3's fixed-size decoder runs out of query tokens beyond ~200 instances.

Recent findings suggest that modern OCR has moved well beyond extracting text from clean scans. Today's systems must handle multi-column layouts, mathematical formulas, tables, charts, and multilingual content — all in one pass. Most competitive OCR VLMs tackle this with a familiar recipe: a vision encoder feeding a separate text decoder, plus task-specific glue. These systems work, but they tend to be large (1B–3B+ parameters).

Sources indicate that we took a different path: reuse the same early-fusion dense Transformer from Falcon Perception, but train a smaller 0.3B-parameter variant from scratch specifically for OCR. The result is Falcon OCR — a single backbone that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space with the same hybrid attention mask (bidirectional for image tokens, causal for text tokens), and switches tasks through prompts rather than additional modules.

Recent findings suggest that we trained from scratch (no multi-teacher distillation) because the visual features OCR needs — fine-grained glyph recognition, stroke-level discrimination — differ substantially from the object-level features useful for segmentation. Starting fresh lets the backbone develop text-optimized representations from the ground up.

Industry observers note that we train on a curated English-language mixture spanning three core tasks: general document text parsing (digital PDFs, old scans, typewritten documents), mathematical and scientific formula recognition, and table structure recognition. The mixture also includes handwriting, real-world scene text, and synthetic samples generated from rendered LaTeX and HTML sources. The training objective is pure next-token prediction on structured text outputs.

Training proceeds in two phases: a long pre-training phase at constant learning rate where the model learns core OCR capabilities across all element types, followed by a short cosine-decay finetuning phase where the learning rate is annealed to near zero.

According to recent reports, we evaluate on olmOCR (binary correctness checks across diverse inputs) and OmniDocBench (continuous metrics over full-page parses). All comparison models are significantly larger and/or use proprietary infrastructure. At 80.3% on olmOCR with only 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is within 1.7 points of the top system and leads all models on Multi-Column (87.1%) and Tables (90.3%). On OmniDocBench it scores 88.64 overall, ahead of DeepSeek OCR v2, GPT 5.2, and Mistral OCR 3.

Recent findings suggest that at 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is roughly 3x smaller than 0.9B-class OCR VLMs, which translates directly into higher serving throughput. Measured on a single A100-80GB with vLLM at high concurrency:.

The compact footprint and vLLM integration (continuous batching, PagedAttention, optimized CUDA kernels) make it practical for large-scale document digitization where millions of pages need processing.

More broadly, these results suggest that the early-fusion single-stack Transformer is a viable alternative to the "vision encoder plus text decoder" recipe for OCR. One backbone, shared parameter space, one decoding interface, and better data and training signals rather than increasingly complex pipelines. We hope this encourages more work in this direction.

Falcon OCR processes images captured under challenging real-world conditions with varying lighting, diverse text semantics (mathematical formulae, structured tables, handwritten notes), and complex document layouts, to produce structured text output.

Click each category below to expand.

Falcon OCR extracts text from handwritten documents and real-world photographs with variable lighting, orientation, and content complexity.

Falcon OCR accurately reproduces cell entries and structural layout from tables of varying formats and complexity.

Falcon OCR correctly transcribes mathematical expressions ranging from simple equations to multi-line derivations with nested operators.

Falcon OCR preserves reading order and structural fidelity when extracting text from documents with multi-column layouts, figures, and footnotes.

The release includes an inference stack built on PyTorch’s FlexAttention, which makes it practical to express the custom attention patterns and efficiently serve packed variable-length sequences.

Recent findings suggest that in our setup on an H100, typical latencies are on the order of ~100ms prefill, ~200ms upsampling (0ms if cached), and ~50ms decode for a handful of instances. (These numbers depend on resolution, sequence length, and the number of predicted instances.).

For the Falcon-OCR model, we also provide a vLLM docker server for fast deployment and MLX integration for Apple-Silicon.

Please check out the github repo for details.

It has been revealed that falcon Perception is intentionally minimal: one backbone, one objective family, and small heads only where outputs are continuous and dense. The working assumption is that most gains should come from data, compute, and training signals, rather than continually expanding the pipeline with specialized modules.

It has been revealed that the architecture doesn't block any obvious scaling path: add more images and harder prompts for better grounding, mix in text-only data for better language, increase context length for denser scenes. It's still just one sequence model.

Falcon Perception is developed by the Falcon Vision Team at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII), Abu Dhabi, UAE.

If you use Falcon-Perception, please cite.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, without a doubt, Nvidia's dominance in the AI hardware market stems not only from the capabilities of its AI accelerators and its vast software ecosystem, but also from its aggressive procurement strategy that effectively denies its rivals access to sufficient production capacity at TSMC and other contractors. The result of his deals is that supply and capacity commitments rose by almost a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter, primarily due to memory procurement, according to SemiAnalysis. However, even Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang had apparently begun to question the sustainability of this strategy before his departure, based on reports from The Wall Street Journal and SemiAnalysis.

Sources indicate that over the past several years, Nvidia has not only captured the vast majority of the AI accelerator market, but has also secured a substantial proportion of the world's production capacity for advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and various other components required to build AI accelerators and systems, which has limited the ability of its competitors to ramp up shipments of their processors. To support the deals, Jensen Huang personally negotiated agreements with major suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.

In a recent development, the massive scale of Nvidia's procurement commitments also enabled the company to secure more favorable quotes than its rivals. SemiAnalysis estimates that SK hynix could charge Nvidia between $3.00 and $3.30 per gigabit of HBM4 memory in 2027, whereas other first-tier customers, such as AMD, Amazon, Broadcom, and Google, would pay between $3.70 and $4.10 per gigabit. The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.

While Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the company's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. As half a trillion dollars seems gargantuan, here is a breakdown based on a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission:.

The scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.

At some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.

It has been revealed that despite questionable commitments, without Huang and his personal relationships with executives at major semiconductor companies, Nvidia may find it harder to secure preferential treatment from its suppliers. SemiAnalysis believes that customers other than Nvidia could account for over 70% of TSMC production capacity in 2028. While this could enable Nvidia’s competitors to significantly increase shipments of their AI processors, it could also affect the willingness of Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers to invest aggressively in additional production capacity without the kind of assurances that Huang used to provide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that betMGM paid MGM $34 million in distributions and brand license fees in the third quarter, while MGM's Las Vegas Strip earnings fell 12%.
  • It has been revealed that MGM Resorts’ third-quarter 2026 results, released October 28, showed its online partner becoming a source of cash as Las Vegas softened.
  • BetMGM sent $68 million in total to its two owners, Entain and MGM, during the quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that betMGM paid MGM $34 million in distributions and brand license fees in the third quarter, while MGM's Las Vegas Strip earnings fell 12%. The online venture's profit rose 112%, but its iGaming growth trailed a slowing US market.

It has been revealed that MGM Resorts’ third-quarter 2026 results, released October 28, showed its online partner becoming a source of cash as Las Vegas softened. MGM now receives both distributions and brand license fees from the venture. On the Strip, lower room rates hurt results.

BetMGM sent $68 million in total to its two owners, Entain and MGM, during the quarter. That sum combined $18 million in parent fees and $50 million in cash distributions. A year earlier, MGM had expected the payments to begin in the fourth quarter of 2025, with an initial payment of at least $100 million.

BetMGM’s net revenue rose 7% to $710 million from $667 million. iGaming accounted for $483 million of that, up 6%. Online sports net revenue reached $216 million, up 7%. Profit grew faster than revenue, with nine-month adjusted EBITDA reaching $185 million.

BetMGM holds 14% of gross gaming revenue across its active markets, including 20% in iGaming and 8% in online sports betting. It kept its 2026 guidance of $2.9 billion to $3.1 billion in net revenue and $300 million to $350 million in adjusted EBITDA. However, it now expects results near the bottom of both ranges.

Its 6% iGaming gain lagged the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, the slowest rate on record, according to Citizens JMP Securities. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. State results varied, with growth of 7% in Pennsylvania, 10% in Newly introduced Jersey and 17% in Michigan.

Regional Operations revenue fell on a reported basis to $883.2 million from $956.9 million. The drop reflects the April 2026 sale of MGM Northfield Park’s operations for $546 million. Removing $83.7 million from sold properties leaves a prior-year same-store base of $873.2 million. Measured against that base, the regional business grew slightly.

Industry observers note that MGM Digital, which includes LeoVegas but not BetMGM, grew revenue to $184 million from $174 million. Its segment adjusted EBITDAR loss narrowed to $4 million from $23 million. CEO Bill Hornbuckle said MGM’s digital businesses delivered strong revenue growth.

Taken together, the figures are consistent with digital operations offsetting part of the weakness on the Strip. The next test for the online market comes from DraftKings, which reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Thursday, November 5. Its conference call follows on Friday, November 6, at 8:30 a.m. ET.

  • In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.
  • One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration.
  • The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

You’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned).

In a recent development, across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing people. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot.

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

Latest Update: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we've heard your concerns about the speed of A2UI and generative UI experiences: people wait while the model generates each screen.
  • It has been revealed that with this release, we’re happy to introduce swappable inference formats and share examples on leveraging decision models with A2UI, which help building faster and more reliable generative UI experiences.
  • A2UI is an agent-optimized protocol for generative UI, where a client advertises a catalog of trusted components as a contract, an agent sends A2UI messages describing a bespoke user interface composed from that catalog, and the client's renderer draws the UI (see Introducing A2UI).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we've heard your concerns about the speed of A2UI and generative UI experiences: people wait while the model generates each screen. This release gives you levers to make that faster, so you can choose the trade-off that fits each screen.

It has been revealed that with this release, we’re happy to introduce swappable inference formats and share examples on leveraging decision models with A2UI, which help building faster and more reliable generative UI experiences. Using our new A2UI Express as an inference format you can reduce latency by up to 3x, and up-to 80x using decision models like Jev to make layout decisions. Express requires up to 3x fewer tokens to generate the same kinds of UI compared to Direct JSON. We'll dive into the details in this blog post.

A2UI is an agent-optimized protocol for generative UI, where a client advertises a catalog of trusted components as a contract, an agent sends A2UI messages describing a bespoke user interface composed from that catalog, and the client's renderer draws the UI (see Introducing A2UI).

Sources indicate that initially agents generated A2UI JSON transport messages directly, every curly brace and nested element. It turns out that generating JSON trees constrained by a complex JSON schema is slow and error-prone for LLMs. This coupled A2UI to LLMs, which output text, and made it difficult to integrate faster System One decision models.

Industry observers note that now agents can generate A2UI Express, an intermediate format optimized for inference speed and accuracy, and rely on deterministic code in A2UI's Agent SDKs to translate it into the JSON-based transport protocol. Agent builders are also free to swap in any other DSL and its associated compiler for any special use-cases, and our A2UI Agent SDK(s) make it compatible with transports and renders.

Industry observers note that the format the model generates is what we call inference_format. You set it with one argument when you create the generator. The SDK generates the prompt instructions for that format and compiles the model's reply into standard A2UI messages. This post covers how the swap works, why we developed A2UI Express as the new default inference format, and how a decision model can build screens from layouts you define in advance.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that these models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device.
  • We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗.

Recent findings suggest that these models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device. Gemma 4 builds on advances from previous families and makes them click together. In our tests with pre-release checkpoints we have been impressed by their capabilities, to the extent that we struggled to find good fine-tuning examples because they are so good out of the box.

We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it. This blog post will show you how to build with your favorite tools so let us know what you think!

Sources indicate that similar to Gemma-3n, Gemma 4 supports image, text, and audio inputs, and generates text responses. The text decoder is based on the Gemma model with support for long context windows. The image encoder is similar to the one from Gemma 3 but with two crucial improvements: variable aspect ratios, and configurable number of image token inputs to find your sweet spot between speed, memory, and quality. All models support images (or video) and text inputs, while the small variants (E2B, E4B) and the 12B Unified model support audio as well.

Gemma 4 comes in five sizes, all base and instruction fine-tuned:.

Gemma 4 leverages several architecture components used in previous Gemma versions and other open models, and leaves out complex or inconclusive features such as Altup. The combination is a mix designed to be highly compatible across libraries and devices, that can efficiently support long context and agentic use cases, whilst being ideal for quantization.

As shown in the benchmarks above, this feature mix (combined with the training data and recipe) enables the 31B dense model to achieve an estimated LMArena score (text only) of 1452, while the 26B MoE reaches 1441 with just 4B active parameters 🤯. As we'll see, multimodal operation is comparatively as good as text generation, at least in informal and subjective tests.

These are the main architecture characteristics in Gemma 4:.

One of the most distinctive features in smaller Gemma 4 models is Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which was introduced previously in Gemma-3n. In a standard transformer, each token gets a single embedding vector at input, and the same initial representation is what the residual stream builds on across all layers, forcing the embedding to frontload everything the model might need. PLE adds a parallel, lower-dimensional conditioning pathway alongside the main residual stream. For each token, it produces a small dedicated vector for every layer by combining two signals: a token-identity component (from an embedding lookup) and a context-aware component (from a learned projection of the main embeddings). Each decoder layer then uses its corresponding vector to modulate the hidden states via a lightweight residual block after attention and feed-forward. This gives each layer its own channel to receive token-specific information only when it becomes relevant, rather than requiring everything to be packed into a single upfront embedding. Because the PLE dimension is much smaller than the main hidden size, this adds meaningful per-layer specialization at modest parameter cost. For multimodal inputs (images, audio, video), PLE is computed before soft tokens are merged into the embedding sequence — since PLE relies on token IDs that are lost once multimodal features replace the placeholders. Multimodal positions use the pad token ID, effectively receiving neutral per-layer signals.

The shared KV cache is an efficiency optimization that reduces both compute and memory during inference. The last num_kv_shared_layers layers of the model don't compute their own key and value projections. Instead, they reuse the K and V tensors from the last non-shared layer of the same attention type (sliding or full).

In practice, this has a minimal impact on quality while being much more efficient (in terms of both memory and compute) for long context generation and on-device use.

The Gemma 4 12B Unified model has no separate vision or audio encoder. Instead, raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the LLM's embedding space through lightweight linear layers, and all modalities flow into a single decoder-only transformer. This reduces multimodal latency and allows the whole model to be fine-tuned in one pass. The checkpoint size makes it deployment-friendly on consumer hardware.

Recent findings suggest that we saw in our tests that Gemma 4 supports comprehensive multimodal capabilities out of the box. We don't know what was the training mix, but we had success using it for tasks such as OCR, speech-to-text, object detection, or pointing. It also supports text-only and multimodal function calling, reasoning, code completion and correction.

According to recent reports, google has released Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafters for the Gemma 4 family: small assistant models that accelerate inference via speculative decoding. The drafter proposes several future tokens at once, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass. You get the same outputs as the target model, just faster — no quality loss, no changes to reasoning behaviour. Reported end-to-end speedups go up to ~3x depending on hardware, batch size, and workload.

Assistants are available for all four Gemma 4 sizes (E2B, E4B, 26B A4B, 31B). They share the KV cache with the target model to avoid recomputing context, and the smaller edge variants additionally use an embedder clustering trick to keep memory and compute low on-device.

Find the checkpoints in the Gemma 4 collection and the mlx-community collection.

Alongside the autoregressive Gemma 4 family, Google DeepMind is releasing DiffusionGemma, a multimodal model that generates text using discrete diffusion instead of token-by-token autoregression. It's built on the same 26B A4B Mixture-of-Experts foundation (25.2B total / 3.8B active parameters, 8 active experts out of 128 plus 1 shared), takes text and image inputs, generates text, and supports up to 256K context — all under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Where a standard causal LM emits one token at a time, DiffusionGemma denoises whole blocks of tokens in parallel. The architecture is encoder-decoder: an autoregressive encoder prefills the prompt and builds the KV cache, while a decoder applies bidirectional attention over a "canvas" of 256 tokens. During multi-canvas sampling, the model iteratively denoises a full canvas with a diffusion sampler; once a canvas is finalized it's encoded and appended to the KV cache, then the next canvas begins. This block-autoregressive approach increases generation speed.

The headline benefit is throughput: parallel denoising generates roughly 15–20 tokens per forward pass, reaching per-user generation speeds exceeding 1100 tokens/second at low batch sizes (H100, FP8). Inference compute is adaptive too — simpler prompts and structured tasks like code need fewer denoising steps, so tokens-per-second scales with task complexity. It keeps the broader Gemma 4 toolkit: thinking mode, function calling, long context, native system prompts, and image understanding (OCR, document parsing, object detection, pointing) at variable aspect ratios and resolutions.

Benchmarks show an expected trade-off between speed and evaluation metrics — DiffusionGemma trails the autoregressive 26B A4B on most tasks (e.g. MMLU Pro 77.6% vs 82.6%, AIME 2026 69.1% vs 88.3%, GPQA Diamond 73.2% vs 82.3%) in exchange for its large speed advantage, while edging ahead on a few (HLE no tools 11.0% vs 8.7%).

Getting started looks just like the rest of Gemma 4, via the dedicated diffusion class:.

In a recent development, for best results, Google recommends the Entropy-Bounded (EB) sampler with adaptive stopping (up to 48 denoising steps, a temperature schedule decaying from 0.8 → 0.4, and an entropy bound of 0.1 for token selection). As with Gemma 4, place image content before text in your prompt, and toggle reasoning with the <|think|> control token.

Gemma 4 models are ideal for fine-tuning in your favorite tools and platforms and at any budget.

Gemma 4 is fully supported for fine-tuning with TRL. To celebrate, TRL has been upgraded with support for multimodal tool responses when interacting with environments, meaning models can now receive images back from tools during training, not just text.

In a recent development, to showcase this, we've built an example training script where Gemma 4 learns to drive in the CARLA simulator. The model sees the road through a camera, decides what to do and learns from the outcome. After training, it consistently changes lanes to avoid pedestrians. The same approach works for any task where a model needs to see and act: robotics, web browsing, or other interactive environments.

Sources indicate that additionally, we have prepared an example on how to fine-tune Gemma 4 with TRL on Vertex AI using SFT, to showcase how to extend the function calling capabilities, whilst freezing both the vision and audio towers. The examples include how to build a custom Docker container with latest Transformers, TRL, etc. with CUDA support on Google Cloud, and how to run it via Vertex AI Serverless Training Jobs.

You can find the complete example in the "Hugging Face on Google Cloud" docs at https://hf.co/docs/google-cloud/examples/vertex-ai-notebooks-fine-tune-gemma-4.

According to recent reports, one gap worth flagging for anyone building on Gemma 4's function calling for real-world deployments: when the model generates a function call, there's at the moment no verifiable record that a human principal authorized that specific action. a compromised system prompt or injected instruction produces a call that's indistinguishable from legitimate delegation at the tool interface.

i opened a PR on the gemma-cookbook repo today that adds a drop-in HDP middleware layer to address this, sits between Gemma 4's function call output and tool execution, verifies Ed25519-signed delegation tokens, classifies actions by irreversibility (Class 0–3), and blocks unauthorized calls pre-execution.

for edge/robotics deployments (E2B on Jetson Nano / Raspberry Pi directing actuators), there's a companion HDP-P extension covering the physical layer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AMVR GA2 is a fresh take on a Quest 3 golf club accessory, and I was pleasantly surprised with what it did for my scores.

It has been revealed that in the past decade of covering VR devices and accessories, I’ve used a lot of golf clubs. Short clubs. Long clubs. Adjustable length clubs. Clubs with realistic weight. Even a club with a magnet inside that makes a convincing “thwack!” sound every time you swing it. But the AMVR GA2’s inclusion of a proper club head at the bottom does something fascinating for its physics, and I immediately noticed the difference at the end of the first course I played with this Quest 3 golf club.

According to recent reports, most VR golf club accessories, including the first-gen AMVR GA1, stick the controller at the bottom of the shaft where the head usually goes. All major VR golf games allow custom spacing for Quest 3 golf clubs, so it doesn’t take more than 30 seconds to get comfortable with the club in your game of choice.

Safetensors is Joining the PyTorch Foundation

📅 08 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.
  • Sources indicate that safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code.
  • The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Sources indicate that safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

We want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single company. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

For the vast majority of consumers, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

The coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

We're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to new features and participation in governance.

In a recent development, if you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an problem, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

According to recent reports, will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both customers and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5.
  • The demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load.
  • Industry observers note that building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both customers and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5. Perhaps as practical proof of that claim, front-end developer Maksymilian Dendura took inspiration from the demoscene and had Fable roll his own virtual underwater world, Abyssal Garden, in only 96 KB of Javascript/HTML — you can check it out here.

The demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load. Using actual meshes and images for textures would otherwise take up a significant amount of space.

Industry observers note that building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly. Some games employ this technique for repeated elements like trees and grass.

Sources indicate that likewise, all the visual effects and even some texturing are done with shaders, which are small programs that change how a mesh or texture appears — for example, to make parts of an object shiny. Games use them extensively, as many players are aware, thanks to endless "loading shaders" screens or Unreal Engine's st-tu-tutering.

The result is definitely impressive, especially but not only as it's purely browser-based, relying on WebGPU and WebGL. Both are rarely-mentioned technologies that have actually existed for a long while now. As their names imply, they let developers render 2D and 3D graphics in a manner similar to that of OpenGL, but in a browser, using JavaScript as the base language.

Recent findings suggest that the demo's most impressive fact is the simplicity of the prompt that got Fable 5.2 to build it. It's only about 40 lines long with word wrapping, and clearly illustrates the degree of autonomy that contemporary agentic AI has when given a specific, yet exceedingly open-ended task like this one. It's reasonable enough to assume the author did a few rounds of tweaking (and he has excellent artistic taste too), but the agent's acumen is nevertheless impressive.

Comparing this demo to an actual game is inevitable, but the reality is that demos have but an atom-sized fraction of the content of a full game, and are limited to little or no interaction, logic, or physics.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that performance is decent for what is a great-looking but otherwise tiny and almost featureless space. The author claims that he's getting 180 FPS at 1440p on an RTX 5070 Ti. Likewise, having this world in 97 KB sounds impressive, but it's actually gigantic for this type of demo, even if an X user further optimized it for 52 KB.

Regular computing customers, including AI neophytes and acolytes, may not be aware that this kind of space-optimized programming for the purposes of visual/aural demonstrations is a discipline and art form that harkens back to the 1980s when 16-bit computers appeared — called the "demoscene.".

It has been revealed that by no means discounting the extraordinary fact that Fable did this nearly all by itself — which is the actual achievement here — code wizards have pulled off nearly impossible feats decades ago, including in browsers. The 2009 demo Elevatedn (17 years ago) has a comparable aesthetic, and includes music, in just under 4 KB (yes, four). There's even a browser version of it, taking up all of 4,777 bytes.

Hartverdrahtet (2012 — 14 years ago) has a highly complex 3D space, again in 4 KB. And old-timers in the audience will remember ".kkrieger", an FPS game prototype that fit in all of 96 KB, including meshes, textures, music, and sound effects... back in 2004.

  • Recent findings suggest that barkley bought into Polymarket before the league told players they could not hold such investments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eagles running back Saquon Barkley sold his equity stake in Polymarket after NFL rules barred players from holding prediction-market investments. The case sets the league apart from the NBA and MLB, which have signed deals with the exchanges, as the NFL argues at the Supreme Court that sports event contracts are gambling.

Saquon Barkley no longer owns a piece of Polymarket. The Eagles running back sold his equity stake to comply with league rules, he told Front Office Sports in an interview published October 28. It is the first public case of the NFL applying its gambling rules to a player’s prediction-market investment.

Recent findings suggest that barkley bought into Polymarket before the league told players they could not hold such investments. The NFL goes over endorsement, investment and training rules with players before every season.

The league has now made clear that its sportsbook restrictions extend to prediction markets. It declined to comment on Barkley’s case specifically. The stance was not new to players. Kalshi and Polymarket were already off-limits to them as endorsers or brand ambassadors in January 2026. At that point, prediction markets were treated as gambling entities under the league’s gambling policy.

Recent findings suggest that the NFL’s approach puts it at odds with other major leagues. Polymarket became Major League Baseball’s Official Prediction Market Exchange on March 19, 2026. On October 26, 2026, the NBA named both companies its preferred prediction-market exchanges. The agreement gives them rights to league intellectual property and marketing.

Sources indicate that NBA players face far lighter limits. They can hold stakes in the exchanges and appear in their marketing. The line is drawn only at promoting contracts on NBA games.

The split also shuts NFL players out of an industry that leans heavily on their sport. By the league’s own figures, football made up $1.8 billion of prediction-market trading on the season’s first Sunday. That was more than half of the day’s total.

The league is pressing that view at the Supreme Court. On October 8, 2026, it filed an amicus brief supporting New Jersey’s request for review in Flaherty v. KalshiEX, case No. 26-299. The NFL argued that sports prediction contracts are gambling. In its view, they are not financial swaps under exclusive federal oversight.

Sources indicate that fresh Jersey filed its petition on September 2, 2026. It followed an April ruling in which the Third Circuit sided 2-1 with Kalshi. The appeals court found that the CFTC has exclusive oversight of sports-event contracts.

Exclusive: Saquon Barkley tells FOS he was forced to divest his equity stake in Polymarket.

NFL players are not allowed to invest in or endorse gambling or prediction market companies.

— Front Office Sports (@FOS) October 28, 2026.

In a recent development, many of the NFL’s concerns will be addressed through the CFTC’s ongoing rulemaking, Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said. In her view, the agency already has the power to police sports-related event contracts.

Sources indicate that the Supreme Court granted Kalshi a 30-day extension to answer New Jersey. Its response, originally due October 8, must now be filed by November 9.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

According to recent reports, for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Industry observers note that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

In a recent development, an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

In a recent development, when you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Recent findings suggest that pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 upgrade, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these latest multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

According to recent reports, VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

It has been revealed that some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

It has been revealed that the model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

Industry observers note that with a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

It has been revealed that you might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

Sources indicate that these methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

The reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

Sources indicate that since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Recent findings suggest that multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

In a recent development, you may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

Recent findings suggest that in Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Recent findings suggest that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Industry observers note that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free initiative is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app owners, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

In a recent development, bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Recent findings suggest that replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web aims run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new consumers $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Recent findings suggest that figma's Starter proposal is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Industry observers note that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human people.

Recent findings suggest that building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Google has been at its gradient redesign schtick for a while now to varying levels of success, but its latest redesign has just landed on the Pixel Watch for the Media Controls app, and I love it.

Quietly rolled out, the Media Controls app on Pixel Watch has picked up a redesign to its app icon, adopting the same gradient look we’ve seen across several other Pixel Watch apps.

According to recent reports, the difference here is that Google’s styling expands beyond a simple coat of paint. The fresh look extends to the edge of the icon with play/pause in the center and a ring indicating playback around the border, just like the actual app itself – the app, to be clear, hasn’t been redesigned.

I’ve personally been a bit mixed on these redesigns, but this one really nails it in my book. I wish Google would do this sort of thing more often. The white borders are nice in some cases, but I very much miss the whimsy of the icons that took up the full size available to them – that mid-2010’s icon was the absolute peak in my opinion.

Pixel Watch has been quietly rolling out more of these icon redesigns in recent months, with the other most recent additions including Alarm, Stopwatch, and Timer from around August/September.

Recent findings suggest that just days after he left the tech giant under a cloud of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might be on his way back to the company he founded. That's after a number of his allies rallied in support for Huang, including influential SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and outspoken Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The pair are just two of those demanding that Nvidia's board has a rethink, hoping that it will choose to "Bring Jensen Back" to the company. Huang is now discussing that possibility, according to a Financial Times report.

"Huang has discussed with confidantes the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter," the report claimed, adding that allies were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley figures to try and lobby for his return.

Industry observers note that huang's resignation from his Nvidia post came after he released a statement confirming his affair, one which could have repercussions far beyond Nvidia itself. U.S. intelligence was reported to believe that the woman involved in an affair with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang (no relation), is a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security, or MSS. Since Jensen Huang admitted to his adultery, it was further alleged that he had a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. That alone would potentially constitute a violation of Nvidia's own code of conduct. But the affair with an alleged Chinese spy is likely to be the most troublesome for the former-but-potentially-returning CEO.

Sources indicate that it's possible that Huang can expect a vote of confidence from U.S. President Donald Trump, with the pair having a good relationship to date. But Trump recently called for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over at Nvidia.

Outside of the White House, Huang has other concerns to deal with. Congress has summoned him to appear before a Select Committee over his affair with the suspected Chinese spy, threatening to subpoena him if necessary.
