#11132. The PR you would have opened yourself

📅 16 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2053 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The PR you would have opened yourself

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness.
  • Sources indicate that we provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers.
  • In 2026, code agents started to actually work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making transformers models available in mlx-lm using a Skill and test harness.

Sources indicate that we provide a Skill and a test harness to help port language models from transformers to mlx-lm, so they become (almost) instantly available the moment they are added to transformers. The Skill is designed to support contributors and reviewers as an aide, not an automation. We explain why we did it, how, and comment about how to meaningfully contribute to open source in the age of agents.

In 2026, code agents started to actually work. What used to be auto-completion at the side of your editor turned into a system that one-shots reasonable solutions from brief specifications. The generated code usually works out of the box, covers what you asked for, and makes reasonable assumptions about details you didn't specify. This is great. As Jensen Huang puts it, we've instantly gone from 30 million to one billion coders in the world. Creative minds are unleashed.

But it forces us to rethink open source.

Industry observers note that take the transformers library as an example. It has hundreds of contributors, is used in thousands of projects, has been downloaded over a billion times. Suddenly, anyone with an agent can instruct it to find some open issue, fix it, and submit a PR. And that's exactly what's happening. Those people feel happy because they are contributing to a great library, but the sad reality is that, most of the time, they don't realize they are not.

Why not? There are two assumptions that agent-generated PRs usually miss.

Codebases like transformers care deeply about the code. It's cool to build projects where it doesn't matter what the code looks like, but transformers is not one of them. Being used by thousands of people, transformers is primarily built as a human-to-human communication method, through code. Model files read top to bottom, because we want practitioners to understand them without jumping through complex abstractions. This permeates throughout the library design and is the reason why, for example, we favor flat hierarchies.

Agents don't have that context. Because design decisions are not explicit, agents suggest refactors to "improve" the codebase by following "best practices", without realizing they are breaking implicit contracts between the library and its consumers. They are verbose, generalize too early, don't notice when a change affects other areas, introduce subtle bugs, break performance. They are also sycophantic, and accept any idea as good and follow it through diligently, including ones a maintainer would have pushed back early on with a terse comment.

In a recent development, A small number of maintainers still has to read every PR, understand it, decide if the design direction is right, identify side effects, and write feedback. PR volume has gone up tenfold, but the amount of maintainers has not (and cannot, because team coordination does not scale).

It has been revealed that transformers is one of the first projects to feel this pressure because of sheer volume, but the same dynamic is happening everywhere. As an example from a different domain, App Store reviewers are swamped because anyone can now build and submit an app, so many do.

The same logic applies to MLX: their maintainers care deeply about the code and read every PR carefully. We wanted to see whether agents could help contributors land high-quality model ports fast, and at the same time support reviewers in their work. Not only do we aspire to produce PRs that could have come from a careful human submission, but we also provide additional artifacts to increase the signal: generation examples, numerical comparisons, and a separate non-agentic test harness for reproducibility.

Sources indicate that another connection between transformers and MLX is that, most times, mlx-lm models are ported from transformers implementations. Because transformers focuses on clarity and readability, it has become the source of truth for model definitions. Downstream contributors wait until the transformers implementations are ready before they port to other frameworks. As a side effect, this is an excellent environment for an agent because it naturally limits the scope: rather than creating an implementation from scratch, the agent relies on transformers code as the source of truth.

This approach supports our goal: when a model lands in transformers, it should be available on MLX shortly after.

We built a Skill that mlx-lm contributors can use to port a model from transformers to MLX. Given a prompt like "convert the olmo_hybrid architecture to MLX", the Skill sets up a virtual environment to work on, discovers and downloads the relevant models from the Hub, reads the transformers modeling code, writes the MLX implementation, and runs a battery of tests. If results don't look right, it debugs and iterates, and does not declare success until it's satisfied.

We designed it to be useful to reviewers as much as contributors.

It has been revealed that for the contributor, the Skill of course handles all the scaffolding: finding model variants on the Hub, diffing their configs to spot parameters that vary across model variants, downloading checkpoints, setting up editable installs of both mlx-lm and transformers. But it also handles the more difficult modeling tasks. It pays attention to salient architecture details and verifies sensitive areas, like RoPE configurations, that may result in hard-to-find bugs. It detects when the config doesn't declare a dtype and infers it from the safetensors metadata header. It runs per-layer comparisons between transformers and MLX to pinpoint exactly where divergence occurs. These are the kinds of checks that only someone with porting experience would think to run.

Industry observers note that for the reviewer, the Skill produces a PR that is upfront about being agent-assisted, but does look like a careful human submission. Reviewers will see that the code follows mlx-lm conventions: idiomatic solutions, no unnecessary comments, no speculative abstractions, no modifications to shared utilities without explicit approval. Given that the code is agent-assisted, we try to include more data than the median PR, to provide as much signal as possible. The PR body includes a report with a summary of the variants and their architectural differences, generation examples, numerical comparisons, dtype verification, per-layer comparisons against the transformers baseline. The PR always discloses that it was agent-assisted, and the Skill will not open it until the contributor has accepted the results.

For verification, the Skill generates a test manifest for a separate, non-agentic test harness that is, by design, easily reproducible and not subject to LLM hallucinations or complacency (more on this below).

According to recent reports, skills are recipes for agents: simple text files with guidelines that steer the model through a complex task. They are not magic; you can achieve the same results via prompting and iteration. But they provide consistency (every run follows the same process, whereas different people would prompt differently), minimize ambiguity and serve as documentation: anyone can read the Skill to understand what it does, identify missing cases and suggest improvements.

We bootstrapped the Skill by porting a model ourselves, in conversation with Claude. I asked it to port GLM 4.7 from transformers to mlx-lm, giving instructions as I would during a normal session. One trick: I pointed Claude at a checkout of mlx-lm from which I had deleted the already-existing implementation, so I could compare the output against the ground truth. After a few iterations I had a working implementation, a conversation that revealed how Claude approached the problem, and the first draft of the Skill, which Claude created as a summary of the process. I edited it heavily, and incorporated the learnings from @gabegoodhart, who kindly shared their own porting conversation for a different model 🙌.

According to recent reports, we repeated this loop several times and the Skill grew. On the technical side, we covered stuff such as RoPE bugs that may produce plausible output that degrades with long sequences, float32 precision contamination that silently kills inference speed (you'd be surprised how frequently these things happen!), config fields that vary across model variants in ways the implementation must handle, distributed inference for super large models that don't fit on a single machine. We taught it how to invoke the hf CLI to discover and download models. Most importantly, we instructed it to run the tests that experienced porters would, and to not declare success until they pass.

It has been revealed that on the cultural side, we covered softer characteristics and explained the conventions that make a PR easy to review: don't use comments to explain code (the reviewer has to parse the comment and the code 🤦‍♂️), never propose refactors, don't touch shared utilities without asking. These rules cost the agent nothing but save the reviewer lots of time.

The end result: the contributor types a prompt, and the Skill produces a PR like this one, plus a test manifest for the external test harness.

The Skill shares a comprehensive results report as part of the PR. All these come from tests the agent runs during conversion, but we didn't want the reviewer to take a leap of faith to accept them. To go a step forward, we created a separate, non-agentic test harness that runs systematic tests on the converted code. This brings a couple of benefits:.

Sources indicate that the test harness is not a CI gate. Some checks are straightforward (is the output dtype correct?), but most are qualitative. Is it normal that a pre-trained model repeats itself in long sequences? Is a 4% relative logits difference against the transformers baseline acceptable? These are judgement calls based on experience with similar architectures. The harness provides useful signal, but it's the reviewer and contributor who still have to make the call.

The Skill is designed for the people who are already opening mlx-lm model PRs, or who would do it manually on their own. It's not meant for mass consumption, because PRs to mlx-lm are rarely accepted on sight. The typical cycle is: contributor opens a PR, reviewers point out improvements, both sides iterate until the quality bar is met. If this is true for expert submissions, it will remain true for agent-assisted ones.

Sources indicate that if you're not prepared to engage in that cycle, you probably shouldn't be opening a PR. The reviewers will make an effort to understand your code (even knowing it was agent-assisted), so you should do the same. Own the code, and be ready to incorporate their feedback. In particular, don't hand reviewer comments back to an agent and post whatever it produces. LLMs double down on their decisions, go on tangents, and don't push back effectively. Once you engage with the reviewer, this becomes a person-to-person conversation, so it's your turn to discuss and be respectful of the time they put in.

You can also use the Skill to learn; you don't need to submit anything until your confidence and experience build. Read the Skill to identify problem areas you weren't aware of: it contains nearly 15 thousand words among the skill file, reference docs and utility scripts. Point it to your own fork of mlx-lm, try a conversion, and compare your output against the accepted implementation once it lands in the official repo. If you do this a few times, you'll learn a lot about transformers, MLX, and language model architectures.

Recent findings suggest that we developed and tested the Skill using Claude Code. The same approach would work with Codex or other coding agents, but we haven't tested them. If you try the Skill in a different environment, please let us know how it goes!

The Skill works well for LLMs in mlx-lm, but there's plenty of room to grow.

Sources indicate that the bottleneck in open source is not typing speed: it's understaning the codebase to change it without breaking the implicit and explicit contracts with consumers. Agents can help in this process, if we teach them what matters. We explored what this looks like in the context of mlx-lm, and hope it's useful for contributors and reviewers to land high-quality model conversions faster!

Thanks a lot to Ben, Shaun, Aritra for reading previous versions of this post and making it so much better 🙌.

We are incredibly indebted to Apple for making MLX an open-source project, and to the community for instantly recognizing its value and contributing enthusiastically 🙏.

All three northeast Indiana counties reject casino, leaving HEA 1038 license with no host

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that voters in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties each rejected inland casino gambling by double digits on November 3.
  • Sources indicate that with the measure defeated, the license created by House Enrolled Act 1038 cannot be granted by the Indiana Gaming Commission.
  • Industry observers note that allen County, where developers were seeking to build, carried the most weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that voters in Allen, DeKalb and Steuben counties each rejected inland casino gambling by double digits on November 3. The single newly introduced license in House Enrolled Act 1038, tied to a project of at least $500 million, now has no county that can host it.

Sources indicate that with the measure defeated, the license created by House Enrolled Act 1038 cannot be granted by the Indiana Gaming Commission. A repeat ballot is also off the table. State law bars a second public question in any county that voted the measure down.

Industry observers note that allen County, where developers were seeking to build, carried the most weight. The county’s election-night summary counted 102,935 votes on the question, with 40.44% in favor. In DeKalb County, 7,374 voters said no. Steuben County recorded 6,234 no votes.

In a recent development, the stakes were substantial. That minimum investment had to cover both the casino and its non-gambling amenities. At least 60% of that had to be spent within two years of the award. The license also carried a $150 million fee to the state, with $50 million of it going to a fund for former host communities hurt by casino closures.

The projected public return was large as well. A study done for the Indiana Gaming Commission estimated that an Allen County casino could generate $204 million in revenue alongside its annual state tax payments. Under the act, 10% of the casino’s tax payments would have gone to the northeast Indiana regional development authority.

It has been revealed that the process hinged on the vote from the start. The commission’s July guidance mentioned it would take applications only for a county or counties where voters approved inland casino gambling. None did.

Recent findings suggest that gaming Commission officials said that with no county passing the referendum, nothing happens, and that any next steps are up to the legislature. That puts operators back in front of lawmakers.

Industry observers note that lawmakers have already redrawn this map once. Instead of creating a new license, a January 22, 2026 committee version of House Bill 1038 would have relocated the Ohio County riverboat license. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations.
  • This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥.
  • Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR — We extend the RLVE framework from single-turn reasoning puzzles to multi-turn, tool-augmented e-commerce conversations. EcomRLVE-GYM provides 8 verifiable environments — product discovery, substitution, cart building, returns, order tracking, policy QA, bundle planning, and multi-intent journeys — each with procedural problem generation, a 12-axis difficulty curriculum, and algorithmically verifiable rewards. We train a Qwen 3 8B model with DAPO over 300 steps and present early results demonstrating that environment scaling and adaptive difficulty transfer to agentic, real-world task completion.

This project originated in the Pytorch OpenEnv Hackathon and is still evolving, follow us for updates 🔥.

Large language models can hold fluent conversations, yet deploying them as shopping assistants reveals a persistent gap: fluency ≠ task completion. A customer who asks "find me a USB-C charger under $25 that ships in two days" needs an agent that invokes the right catalog search, filters on three hard constraints, avoids hallucinating product IDs it never retrieved, and handles follow-ups when the top result goes out of stock.

Supervised fine-tuning can teach surface-level tool use from demonstrations, but it cannot scale to the combinatorial space of constraint configurations, partial-information dialogues, and multi-step transactional workflows that real e-commerce demands.

According to recent reports, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers an alternative: the agent optimises for outcomes — did the products satisfy the constraints? Was the cart correct? Was the return initiated for the right order line? The challenge is constructing reward functions that are both verifiable (no LLM-as-a-judge subjectivity) and adaptive (difficulty that grows with the policy's capability).

RLVE-Gym provides 400 environments for sorting, multiplication, Sudoku, and other algorithmic-reasoning tasks; however, those are all single-turn, text-in / text-out puzzles — extending to agentic domains was left as future work.

EcomRLVE-GYM fills that gap: we stay in the verifiable regime (e-commerce outcomes can be checked algorithmically) while extending to multi-turn, tool-augmented, agentic conversations — environments where the agent must act (call tools, modify world state) rather than merely reason (produce a text answer) and compensates for the deficiency of the search system.

EcomRLVE-GYM transforms customer-service outcomes structurally verifiable:.

According to recent reports, every signal above can be evaluated by a program with access to the hidden ground-truth goal. No human annotation or LLM-as-a-judge is needed.

According to recent reports, before we explain the framework, here is what a single EcomRLVE episode looks like at difficulty d = 4. The environment generates a hidden goal, a simulated user opens the chat, and the agent must use tools to satisfy the request. Every action is verified algorithmically — no LLM judge required.

In a recent development, the reward is fully computed by code: F1 over (product, variant, qty) tuples, an efficiency bonus for finishing in fewer turns, and a hallucination check that every recommended product ID was actually retrieved. If the agent had picked the Lightning variant instead of USB-C, the simulated user would have corrected it mid-dialogue — and the F1 would have dropped.

Each environment covers a distinct real-world shopping scenario. The agent must complete the task using tools (catalog search, cart operations, order lookups, policy queries) and is scored by a program — not a human or another LLM.

Every environment uses the same three-part reward signal:.

Invalid outputs (malformed JSON, illegal tool calls) trigger an immediate failure score, creating a strong incentive for well-formed responses from step one.

Industry observers note that A single difficulty number d controls 12 independent aspects of a task simultaneously. This is key because e-commerce conversations are hard in many different ways at once — not just along one dimension.

Here are four representative difficulty axes:.

The other eight axes cover turn budget, input noise (typos, slang), context switches, retrieval depth, order-history size, policy complexity, and tool budget. The full breakdown is in the technical report.

Adaptive scheduling. Each environment tracks the agent's success rate independently and only advances to harder problems once the agent is passing the current level reliably. This keeps every environment training at the agent's capability frontier — avoiding both "too easy to learn from" and "too hard to make progress on".

Cart building is a good showcase because it requires the full search → inspect → clarify → act loop, has a binary ground truth, and introduces a challenge absent from most recommendation benchmarks: variant selection.

To succeed, the agent must develop five distinct skills:.

The agent uses six tools to accomplish this:.

The generator samples 1–5 target products (scaling in difficulty with d), each potentially requiring a specific variant (USB-C vs Lightning, Matte vs Glossy) and a quantity > 1. The agent must:.

In a recent development, real product catalogs have sparse variant data — many products have none, and those that do typically vary only by colour or size. To create a richer discrimination task, we synthesize variants at episode initialization:.

At d = 0 the agent adds a single product with no variant complexity — learning the basic catalog.search → cart.add workflow. At d = 6 it juggles 3 items, nearly all requiring a specific variant, with half needing qty > 1.

The cart must be exactly right — correct product, correct variant, correct quantity. Partial credit is given for partially correct carts, but a perfect score requires every item to match. If the agent adds the wrong variant, the simulated user corrects it mid-dialogue ("that's the Lightning version, but I need USB-C"), giving the agent a chance to self-correct before the episode ends.

Two real E_CART episodes from a Qwen 3 8B agent. Same environment, same agent — difficulty alone changes the game.

At d=1 the agent solves the task in 3 clean turns. At d=8 it spirals — picking Bamboo instead of Charcoal, XL instead of XS, never fixing the air fryer despite two user corrections, then hallucinating that the variant doesn't exist. This is exactly the kind of multi-step error cascade that the difficulty curriculum surfaces, and that adaptive training should teach the agent to recover from.

A verifiable environment needs a user simulator that behaves realistically. We use Qwen3.5 (9.7B) to generate natural, varied user messages rather than canned templates — covering everything from typo-filled requests to mid-conversation topic switches.

Two design choices matter for training quality:.

Industry observers note that preferences match stated constraints. Each simulated user has a hidden set of preferences (price sensitivity, brand loyalty, shipping speed, etc.). These are deliberately biased toward whatever constraints the user communicated — so if the user mentioned "under $25", the reward function actually cares about price. Without this, an agent could be penalised for correctly following the user's instructions.

Recent findings suggest that strategic omission. The LLM deliberately withholds some constraints from the opening message to force the agent to ask clarifying questions. The system tracks exactly what was and wasn't mentioned, so the agent is never penalised for information it was never given.

Following RLVE's methodology, we define nested environment collections:.

We hypothesise — consistent with RLVE's findings — that C8 agents outperform single-environment specialists, even on the specialist's own task.

We trained Qwen 3 8B with DAPO on C1 (Cart Building) for 300 steps as an initial viability study.

We saw progressive growth in difficulty reached, confirming that adaptive scheduling produces a steady learning signal rather than the saturation (static-low) or starvation (static-high) patterns predicted by the RLVE paper.

Overlocker uses vibecoded BIOS modification to target Intel's non-K overclocking restrictions

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an attempt to resurrect ASRock's discontinued SkyOC overclocking feature, an enthusiast has vibe-coded a motherboard BIOS using AI, potentially bringing non-K CPU overclocking to modern Intel CPUs.
  • In a recent development, for context, Intel offers multiplier-based overclocking only on its unlocked K-series processors like the Core i9-14900K and the newer Core Ultra 270K Plus.
  • ASRock's SkyOC technology, which was introduced for Intel's Skylake processors in 2016, allowed consumers to overclock locked non-K CPUs through BCLK adjustments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an attempt to resurrect ASRock's discontinued SkyOC overclocking feature, an enthusiast has vibe-coded a motherboard BIOS using AI, potentially bringing non-K CPU overclocking to modern Intel CPUs. According to a post on X, Hardware 360º used Chat-GPT Astra to decompile and compare two versions of an ASRock BIOS, one released with SkyOC and another with the feature disabled. The AI reportedly identified the code responsible for enabling the overclocking workaround and modified it to create a BIOS ready for implementation on a compatible motherboard. Unfortunately, it remains to be seen whether the modified firmware can restore SkyOC on modern Intel platforms, as the workaround is yet to be fully tested.

In a recent development, for context, Intel offers multiplier-based overclocking only on its unlocked K-series processors like the Core i9-14900K and the newer Core Ultra 270K Plus. Non-K models have locked multipliers, which restrict users from pushing CPU frequencies. However, there’s another way to raise the speed of a processor by pushing the base clock itself. The base clock, or BCLK, typically runs at 100 MHz and works alongside the CPU multiplier to determine its operating frequency. For example, raising the base clock speed of a CPU to 105 MHz increases the clock speed by 5%. The only downside is that BCLK adjustments can also affect the entire motherboard, including memory and PCIe-based components, thereby potentially causing system instability.

ASRock's SkyOC technology, which was introduced for Intel's Skylake processors in 2016, allowed consumers to overclock locked non-K CPUs through BCLK adjustments. Certain motherboards also featured independent clock generators, allowing CPU clock adjustments without affecting the rest of the system. Intel was not particularly pleased with the workaround, and ASRock eventually had to remove SkyOC from its motherboards via BIOS updates. Additionally, Intel introduced microcode changes to prevent non-K overclocking.

Sources indicate that the current experiment revisits that workaround by identifying the original BIOS code and adapting it for modern motherboards. Hardware 360º claims Intel's restrictions include a mechanism that triggers a shutdown when BCLK exceeds 103 MHz, and that SkyOC originally worked around this by tricking the processor with a false report of the actual BCLK value.

Sources indicate that finding the original code for SkyOC does not necessarily mean it can be successfully ported to a modern motherboard BIOS. Newer Intel processors use different firmware, microcode, and clock-management mechanisms, which would make adapting the workaround considerably more complicated. Flashing modified motherboard firmware also comes with its own set of risks, including the possibility of rendering the board completely unusable. Nevertheless, it is interesting to see how AI-assisted reverse engineering can help gain access to BIOS modifications that would otherwise require a considerable amount of effort.

Tech Report: How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Recent findings suggest that A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Recent findings suggest that A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

According to recent reports, the bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Industry observers note that each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:.

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

Industry observers note that the first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

Sources indicate that api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:.

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a upcoming connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

In a recent development, node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

In a recent development, the fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:.

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:.

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

According to recent reports, this advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

It has been revealed that each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:.

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:.

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:.

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Sources indicate that logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

According to recent reports, before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

#11123. AI and the Future of Cybersecurity: Why Openness Matters

📅 21 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1092 w)

AI and the Future of Cybersecurity: Why Openness Matters

📅 21 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a new era of cybersecurity.
  • Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things).
  • What Mythos demonstrates is that the following system recipe is powerful:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the announcement of Mythos and Project Glasswing, institutions throughout the world are grappling with the potential dawn of a new era of cybersecurity. In this post, we break down the current situation, discuss the role of openness, and situate the future of cybersecurity within the larger AI ecosystem.

Mythos is a “frontier AI model”, a large language model (LLM) that can be used to process software code (among many other things). This follows a general trend in LLM development, where LLM performance on code-related tasks has recently skyrocketed. What’s particularly significant about Mythos is the system it’s embedded within: It's the system, not the model alone, that has enabled Mythos to rapidly find and patch software vulnerabilities. Understanding this distinction is key to understanding the current landscape of AI cybersecurity.

What Mythos demonstrates is that the following system recipe is powerful:.

Together, these ingredients can uncover software vulnerabilities, find exploits, and build patches. It’s in this recipe — not in any one model — that both the benefits and the risks come in.

Industry observers note that this matters because others can build comparable systems. Smaller models embedded in systems built with deep security expertise could potentially produce similar outcomes more cheaply, which is particularly promising for defense. AI cybersecurity capability is jagged: It doesn’t scale smoothly with model size or general benchmark performance. The system the model is embedded within matters a lot.

According to recent reports, so what Mythos has demonstrated is that it’s possible to build an AI system that finds and addresses software vulnerabilities. We already knew this was possible and there has been increasing work on this, but we’re just beginning to explore what it means in the context of agentic AI: Systems that can rapidly and autonomously take action.

As autonomous systems that identify software vulnerabilities proliferate (and they will), open code and tooling can help level the playing field. Software security has become a speed race across four stages: detection, verification, coordination, and patch propagation. Open ecosystems distribute these across a community, where more closed-source projects centralize knowledge and action across all four stages inside a single vendor, representing a single point of failure where only one organization can see and fix the code. The distributed nature of open development is robust to such constraints, and can be especially powerful in communities with dedicated security professionals, like the Linux kernel security team, the Open Source Security Foundation, and the team at Hugging Face working on model and supply-chain security.

It has been revealed that A common argument for more closed systems is proprietary obscurity, where the code underlying a system is inaccessible. Unfortunately, this provides less protection than it used to. AI systems are increasingly able to assist with reverse engineering of stripped binaries, which matters because most legacy firmware and embedded code is closed, binary-only, and no longer maintained. That code represents a huge attack surface, and it’s becoming more legible and accessible as AI tools improve.

Sources indicate that there’s also a risk created by how AI is being used inside closed codebases. When companies adopt AI coding tools under the wrong incentives (for instance, evaluating engineers by the volume of features shipped rather than code quality) AI-accelerated development can introduce more vulnerabilities into proprietary code than traditional development would. Those vulnerabilities then sit inside a closed codebase where only one organization can find and fix them, while AI-enabled attackers are increasingly capable of discovering them from the outside. The combination of more vulnerabilities produced more quickly, behind a single-organization firewall, is exactly the kind of imbalance that open ecosystems are positioned to avoid.

Underlying all of this is capability asymmetry between attackers and defenders. Open models and open tooling narrow that gap by giving defenders access to the same class of capabilities attackers can reach for — capabilities that would otherwise be concentrated within a small number of well-resourced entities.

Recent findings suggest that cybersecurity defense is where open source and AI agents can play a key role together. Based on the System Card, it appears that Mythos is capable of operating with close to full autonomy, something we’ve advised against due to the potential loss of control. AI agents that are instead semi-autonomous, where the types of actions they can take are prespecified and certain steps require human approval, hit a sweet spot of benefit and risk. In semi-autonomous systems, people remain in control, and the AI agent is responsible for specific subtasks. This is possible to do with open code that organizations can run privately within their own institutions, specifying allowable tools, skills, and system access privileges. With this setup, AI agents can be deployed defensively, finding vulnerabilities and assisting with patching under an organization’s own controls.

The semi-autonomous approach depends on humans being able to actually understand what an AI agent did and why. That’s much more possible when the system is built on open components, such as open agent scaffolding, open rule engines, and auditable decision logs and traces, than when it’s a black box. The “human in the loop” is only meaningful if the human can see into the loop.

Companies don’t have to build these capabilities entirely from scratch. There’s a rich open-source ecosystem of security tooling, including vulnerability scanners, intrusion detection systems, log analyzers, and fuzzing frameworks, that AI agents can be integrated with.

Industry observers note that for high-stakes organizations, starting from open, auditable foundations means security teams can actually inspect how their monitoring works, rather than trusting a single vendor’s claims. This is particularly important where sensitive data and processes are involved, and where sensitive material should generally not be flowing through external AI providers. Open systems can be rigorously analyzed by in-house security professionals, fine-tuned on an organizations’s own secure data, modified to produce organization-specific oversight mechanisms, and run entirely within an organization’s own infrastructure, keeping everything behind appropriate firewalls.

According to recent reports, attackers will develop models that take advantage of vulnerabilities. A significant part of the answer is leaning into transparent practices: open security reviews, published threat models, shared vulnerability databases, and open tooling that any team can adopt. The alternative of each organization trying to secure itself in isolation with proprietary tools doesn’t scale against attackers who are coordinating and sharing techniques in their own communities.

The future of AI cybersecurity will be shaped less by any single model and more by the ecosystems that surround them. Openness provides defenders with the visibility, the control, the community, and the shared infrastructure to stay ahead.

Industry News: Anthropic says Claude Mythos Preview cut AMD MI355X onboarding from up to 12 months to around three days

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic told IPO investors that its Claude Mythos Preview model did the software work required to get its AI running on AMD’s GPUs in about three days, with “basically no human intervention,” a job it states used to take six to 12 months.
  • Tom Brown, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief compute officer, made the time comparison, noting to investors that the original meant using a team of “dozens of engineers.” The organization already runs its models on multiple kinds of chips — on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD, Google’s TPUs, and AWS Trainium — and its fleet is managed as “one fungible pool of compute.” Brown called the early multi-chip decision “an unconventional bet.” It may have been a wise one, given that Google’s TPUs can now natively run AI models built in PyTorch, and Meta uses them in production.
  • It has been revealed that anthropic's claim that the job used to take six to 12 months comes from past work, from its “historical experience bringing up upcoming accelerators using traditional engineering approaches,” where tailoring the code to each hardware platform was a challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic told IPO investors that its Claude Mythos Preview model did the software work required to get its AI running on AMD’s GPUs in about three days, with “basically no human intervention,” a job it states used to take six to 12 months. The three days cover prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs “at a useful level of performance,” with Mythos porting or writing “almost 100% of the kernels.” That kind of low-level code, which ties an AI model to one organization’s chips, has long been part of Nvidia’s CUDA moat, and an AI that can write it in days would suggest that moat is eroding.

Tom Brown, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief compute officer, made the time comparison, noting to investors that the original meant using a team of “dozens of engineers.” The organization already runs its models on multiple kinds of chips — on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD, Google’s TPUs, and AWS Trainium — and its fleet is managed as “one fungible pool of compute.” Brown called the early multi-chip decision “an unconventional bet.” It may have been a wise one, given that Google’s TPUs can now natively run AI models built in PyTorch, and Meta uses them in production.

It has been revealed that anthropic's claim that the job used to take six to 12 months comes from past work, from its “historical experience bringing up upcoming accelerators using traditional engineering approaches,” where tailoring the code to each hardware platform was a challenge. Removing that onboarding barrier could reduce things to a purchase decision, and Anthropic started working with AMD GPUs for the first time this year, with an agreement for up to 2 gigawatts now in place.

According to recent reports, CUDA, Nvidia’s programming platform, is very mature at nearly two decades old. AMD has an equivalent, ROCm, with HIP as its programming layer. Code written for CUDA has to be transformed to work there, and AMD even built a tool called HIPify for the process. There is still a conversion cost to switching, and AMD’s vice president of AI software, Anush Elangovan, told EE Times in April that “Claude is better than HIPify because it has web search built in.”.

It has been revealed that AMD has been making the argument that AI can write this type of code since August of last year, presenting a research agent that fell short of human experts at the time. In September of that year, AMD CEO Lisa Su said on the Possible podcast that much of AI software is written in CUDA, which needs to be “translated to AMD,” and “a ton of that can now be done in software.”.

Moving forward to July earlier this year, AMD’s senior vice president of AI, Vamsi Boppana, noted its engineers were using AI models to generate GPU kernels, and Su said that when she asked whether her team was helping the Anthropic engineer working on the MI355X, she was told they didn’t need any help. Boppana said that in some cases, the resulting kernels were even “better than the most manually tuned versions.” Under its July agreement with Anthropic, AMD is also using Claude to optimize workloads for its Instinct GPUs and to speed up ROCm development.

At AMD’s Advancing AI event in July, OpenAI’s Philippe Tillet said that once OpenAI got its Helios racks, a single engineer confirmed everything worked within a few days, and that “agents are taking over our jobs, in a sense, as kernel engineers.” Before the event, AMD’s Andrew Dieckman, corporate vice president and general manager of the company’s data center GPU business, told reporters that he has had practically zero conversations with AMD’s customers about CUDA.

Published GEAK, an AI agent that writes GPU kernels; against 30 expert-written kernels it got 19 right, at 0.92 times the experts’ speed on average.

Asked about AI coding tools, remarked much of the code written for CUDA can now be translated to AMD in software: “We’re using software to significantly optimize our customers’ code so that they can run on AMD”.

Anush Elangovan, AMD vice president of AI software.

Compared Claude with HIPify, AMD’s tool for converting CUDA code: “Claude is better than HIPify because it has web search built in”.

“We use a ton of AI to create the kernels that we have”; “nobody knows our architecture better than we do”.

Andrew Dieckman, AMD corporate vice president and general manager, data center GPU business.

“I have almost zero conversations with our customers about CUDA at this point in time”.

PC Gamer, from a pre-event AMD briefing.

Vamsi Boppana, AMD senior vice president of AI.

AI-assisted GPU programming will “remove any remaining barriers to broad adoption”.

“agents are taking over our jobs, in a sense, as kernel engineers”.

Tom Brown, Anthropic co-founder and chief compute officer.

One engineer asked Claude to bring up an MI355X rack and left it running “over the weekend”.

Tom Brown, Anthropic co-founder and chief compute officer.

Mythos “got Claude running on AMD in just three days with basically no human intervention”; the slide footnote limits the three days to prompt processing for one model.

Until this week, though, all of this came from AMD or its stage, not from Anthropic to its own investors. Anthropic buys the chips rather than selling them, and it’s heading into its IPO next week, so its multi-chip approach — now with at least some numbers to back it up — carries more weight than a chipmaker’s claims. Its prospectus says it in writing, too, though without a number: “We can onboard latest chip platforms in a fraction of the time it once took.”.

AMD’s Advancing AI keynote, July 23.

Not stated; left running “over the weekend”.

Its “leading model” on an MI355X rack, with performance climbing.

According to recent reports, IPO roadshow video, narration, Nov. 10.

Mythos, with “basically no human intervention”.

Three days (“in just three days”).

Getting “Claude running on AMD”; Claude “ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels”.

Work that “took dozens of engineers months”.

It has been revealed that IPO roadshow video, slide footnote, Nov. 10.

About three days (“~3 day timeline”).

Bringing up “prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs at a useful level of performance”.

Six to 12 months (“~6-12-month estimate”), from “historical experience bringing up upcoming accelerators”.

In a recent development, prospectus (S-1/A No. 2), Nov. 10.

Its engineering teams, “leveraging Claude”.

Bringing “latest chip platforms into production”; no chip named.

What it calls “intense engineering effort over many months”.

The prompt processing (prefill) part of the workload is the step where a model reads and processes what it’s been given before it starts replying, and Anthropic hasn’t said whether the replying step (decode) was included as well. Anthropic’s chart, with its axis labeled “Time to onboard latest silicon,” shows both lines reaching the same “~100%” mark without saying 100% of what. The company also hasn’t said how fast the model ran on AMD’s GPUs versus Nvidia’s, and that’s the comparison we want to see to show whether AMD’s chips, running AI-written code, can match Nvidia silicon.

On the other hand, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang remarked in an April interview with Dwarkesh Patel that Nvidia already uses AI on its own kernels and knows its chips best — “nobody knows our architecture better than we do” — and can get the most out of them. Asked why labs like Anthropic use other accelerators, he called Anthropic “a unique instance, not a trend.” Nvidia and AMD, among seven companies, are buying $26.0 billion of Anthropic’s stock at the IPO price, so Nvidia is investing in the very company Huang called the exception.

In late July, SemiAnalysis published an article, “Can AMD break the CUDA Moat?,” which essentially mentioned that software creation is not the same moat it was even a year ago. That said, the catch for AMD is that with agentic coding, “each agent requires GPUs to test their code against,” which means that the AI writing the code still needs the hardware. It has found a constant lack of GPUs inside AMD for this type of development, which has held AMD back and may be a latest bottleneck.

Sources indicate that that leaves CUDA’s moat somewhere in between. Getting a model running on a new chip, once the expensive part, appears to be getting cheaper, and better AI may wear down Nvidia’s claim that it knows its hardware best. As for Anthropic’s fungible pool, the chips in it aren’t fully interchangeable — Google’s TPUs are increasingly specialized, for example — and getting the most out of any of them still takes the hardware to test on. The moat is narrowing, but is not gone.

According to recent reports, anthropic’s first AMD MI450 chips, in Helios racks, are expected in the first half of 2027. That’s a new generation and an opportunity to see if the three-day bring-up can be repeated. Anthropic’s IPO comes sooner, after which it will report as a public tech giant.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • QIMMA validates benchmarks before evaluating models, ensuring reported scores reflect genuine Arabic language capability in LLMs.
  • If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?
  • Industry observers note that we built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

QIMMA validates benchmarks before evaluating models, ensuring reported scores reflect genuine Arabic language capability in LLMs.

🏆 Leaderboard · 🔧 GitHub · 📄 Paper.

If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?

Industry observers note that we built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically. Instead of aggregating existing Arabic benchmarks as-is and running models on them, we applied a rigorous quality validation pipeline before any evaluation took place. What we found was sobering: even widely-used, well-regarded Arabic benchmarks contain systematic quality problems that can quietly corrupt evaluation results.

This post walks through what QIMMA is, how we built it, what problems we found, and what the model rankings look like once you clean things up.

Arabic is spoken by over 400 million people across diverse dialects and cultural contexts, yet the Arabic NLP evaluation landscape remains fragmented. A few key pain points have motivated this work:.

Translation problems. Many Arabic benchmarks are translations from English. This introduces distributional shifts. Questions that feel natural in English become awkward or culturally misaligned in Arabic, making benchmark data less representative of how Arabic is naturally used.

Absent quality validation. Even native Arabic benchmarks are often released without rigorous quality checks. Annotation inconsistencies, incorrect gold answers, encoding errors, and cultural bias in ground-truth labels have all been documented in established resources.

According to recent reports, reproducibility gaps. Evaluation scripts and per-sample outputs are rarely released publicly, making it hard to audit results or build on prior work.

Coverage fragmentation. Existing leaderboards cover isolated tasks and narrow domains, making holistic model assessment difficult.

To illustrate where QIMMA sits relative to existing platforms:.

QIMMA is the only platform combining all five properties: open source, predominantly native Arabic content, systematic quality validation, code evaluation, and public per-sample inference outputs.

QIMMA consolidates 109 subsets from 14 source benchmarks into a unified evaluation suite of over 52,000 samples, spanning 7 domains:.

A few things stand out about this design:.

According to recent reports, this is the methodological heart of QIMMA. Before running a single model, we applied a multi-stage validation pipeline to every sample in every benchmark.

Each sample was independently evaluated by two state-of-the-art LLMs:.

We chose two models with strong Arabic capability but different training data compositions, so that their combined judgment is more robust than either alone.

Each model scores a sample against a 10-point rubric, with binary scores (0 or 1) per criterion:.

A sample is eliminated if either model scores it below 7/10. Samples where both models agree on elimination are dropped immediately. However, where only one model flags a sample, it proceeds to human review in Stage 2.

Flagged samples are reviewed by native Arabic speakers with cultural and dialectal familiarity. Human annotators make final calls on:.

For culturally sensitive content, multiple perspectives are considered, since "correctness" can genuinely vary across Arab regions.

The pipeline revealed recurring quality challenges across benchmarks; not isolated errors, but systematic patterns reflecting gaps in how benchmarks were originally constructed.

False or mismatched gold indices, factually wrong answers, missing or raw text answers.

Corrupt or illegible text, spelling and grammar errors, and duplicate samples.

Stereotype reinforcement and monolithic generalizations about diverse communities.

Misalignment of gold answers with evaluation protocols.

Sources indicate that code benchmarks required a different intervention. Rather than discarding samples, we refined the Arabic problem statements in 3LM's Arabic adaptations of HumanEval+ and MBPP+, leaving task identifiers, reference solutions, and test suites completely unchanged.

The modification rates were striking:.

Modifications fell into five categories:.

QIMMA uses LightEval, EvalPlus and FannOrFlop as its evaluation framework, chosen for consistency, multilingual community adoption, and reproducibility.

QIMMA standardizes prompting by question format, with six template types:.

Industry observers note that all prompts are in Arabic. For MizanQA and ArabCulture, benchmark-specific system prompts from the original papers are preserved.

Results as of April 2026; covering top 10 evaluated models. Visit the live leaderboard for current rankings.

The VGW complaint puts a dollar figure on the state's sweepstakes market and adds Arkansas to a growing list of states challenging the dual-currency model.

One lawsuit targets VGW, the company behind Chumba Casino, LuckyLand and Global Poker. The other targets KalshiEX LLC and Kalshi Inc., the companies that own the Kalshi prediction market.

Both cases allege illegal gambling and violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Both also include an unjust enrichment claim. In each case the state seeks restitution, penalties, taxes and injunctive relief.

The VGW suit attacks the Gold Coin/Sweeps Coin model that almost every US sweepstakes casino relies on. It names ten affiliated VGW companies. The complaint notes VGW reported about $66 million in taxable Arkansas sales between July 2025 and June 2026 and paid about $6 million in sales and use tax over that period, Gaming.net reported.

It has been revealed that those figures show a company declaring sales to the state and paying tax on them. Yet VGW holds no Arkansas casino license, the state alleges. The complaint also accuses VGW of letting 18-year-olds play, even though Arkansas casinos require players to be 21.

The case lands less than two months after the Upcoming York settlement. New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed that deal on September 9, 2026. It covered Chumba Casino, Global Poker and Luckyland Slots. VGW’s coin-based games were already off the table for New Yorkers by then, after her office sent the manufacturer a cease-and-desist letter in June 2025.

Sources indicate that kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman went to court a few months earlier, claiming VGW’s sweepstakes casinos break Kentucky gambling law. Florida has also moved against dual-currency sweepstakes since June 2026. Arkansas now joins Kentucky, Florida and Fresh York on that list. For operators using the same coin structure, the pattern points to rising legal exposure state by state.

The Kalshi complaint rests on a constitutional definition. The Arkansas Constitution’s definition of casino gaming expressly covers accepting wagers on sporting events. Kalshi has never held a casino-gaming license from the state commission, the state alleges. Nor has it held any other Arkansas authorization to take sports wagers.

In a recent development, the complaint expressly limits itself to state-law claims and relief under Arkansas law. That choice means the state is relying on its own consumer-protection statute rather than waiting on the CFTC. Money lost, betting that gets out of hand, and depression or other damage to mental health are dangers Kalshi understands its customers face, Griffin’s office said.

Today I filed a lawsuit against VGW, an online gaming platform that features such games as @ChumbaCasino, LuckyLand Casino, @LuckyLandSlots, and @official_glp.

Industry observers note that arkansas’s gambling laws are clear. If you’re providing a means for Arkansans to gamble money within our state, you are… pic.twitter.com/qs2dhRMC8K.

— Attorney General Tim Griffin (@AGTimGriffin) November 4, 2026.

In a recent development, filing both cases on the same day signals how Arkansas views the two products. The attorney general is treating sweepstakes casinos and sports event contracts as the same kind of unlicensed gambling. Other states may weigh whether to copy that approach.

The VGW case was filed in White County Circuit Court. The Kalshi case was filed in Independence County Circuit Court.

After being barebones at launch, Google is improving on Pixel 11 Pro’s Hilight feature with message support, now including WhatsApp.

As a part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop that was released this week, Google Messages added support for HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro series. As we reported back in September when Google started beta testing the functionality, owners can select a contact and enable a specific color light for phone calls and/or messages.

Industry observers note that am I that old, or does no one else remember when Blackberry had a colored light that could be configured to run a rainbow of different colors with different patterns for any app notification. What's old is fresh again....

Google’s announcement only officially introduced support for the Google Messages app but, as it turns out, WhatsApp is also supported.

It has been revealed that shenaz Zack, Senior Director of Product Management over Pixel, confirmed through a brief video on Twitter/X that WhatsApp messages can also now activate HiLight. This isn’t a huge surprise given WhatsApp calls have been supported since day one, but it’s a nice addition for the many users who prefer WhatsApp over SMS/RCS.

HiLight already worked with WhatsApp calls and now, it works with WhatsApp messages, too, doing the heavy lifting so my favorites get the VIP attention 😄 pic.twitter.com/ouLROk1FeF.

Android 17 QPR2 enables the patch, and it’s rolling out now to all Pixel 11 Pro devices.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.
  • While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.
  • This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.

While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.

This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.

By the end, you will have the same architecture used in this project: a background service worker that hosts models, a side panel chat UI, and a content script for page-level actions.

In this guide, we will recreate the core architecture of Transformers.js Gemma 4 Browser Assistant, using the published extension as a reference and the open-source codebase as the implementation map.

Before diving in, a quick scope note: I will not go deep on the React UI layer or Vite build configuration. The focus here is the high-level architecture decisions: what runs in each Chrome runtime and how those pieces are orchestrated.

If Manifest V3 is new to you, read this short overview first: What is Manifest V3?.

Recent findings suggest that in MV3, your architecture starts in public/manifest.json. This project defines three entry points:.

Sources indicate that the background service worker also handles chrome.action.onClicked to open the side panel for the active tab. Related entry point to know: a popup can be defined with action.default_popup and works well for quick actions. This project uses a side panel for persistent chat, but the orchestration pattern is the same.

The key design decision is to keep heavy orchestration in the background and keep UI/page logic thin.

One practical consequence of this division is that the conversation history also lives in background (Agent.chatMessages): the UI sends events like AGENT_GENERATE_TEXT, background appends the message, runs inference, then emits MESSAGES_UPDATE back to the side panel.

This split avoids duplicate model loads, keeps the UI responsive, and respects Chrome's security boundaries around DOM access.

It has been revealed that once runtimes are separated, messaging becomes the backbone. In this project, all messages are typed through enums in src/shared/types.ts.

The orchestration rule is simple: the background is the single coordinator; side panel and content script are specialized workers that request actions and render results.

In src/shared/constants.ts, this extension uses two model roles:.

The split is intentional: Gemma 4 handles reasoning/tool decisions, while MiniLM generates vector embeddings for the semantic similarity search in ask_website and find_history.

All inference runs in background (src/background/background.ts):.

According to recent reports, this gives a single model host for all tabs/sessions, avoids duplicate memory usage, and keeps the side panel UI responsive. Because models are loaded from the background service worker, artifacts are cached under the extension origin (chrome-extension://) rather than per-website origins, which gives one shared cache for the whole extension install.

MV3 lifecycle note: service workers can be suspended and restarted, so model runtime state should be treated as recoverable and re-initialized when needed.

The model lifecycle is explicit:.

Permissions and privacy are part of the architecture, not a checkbox at the end. In this project, public/manifest.json asks for sidePanel, storage, scripting, and tabs, plus host_permissions for http(s)://*/*:.

Why keep this narrow: permissions define user trust and Chrome Web Store review risk. Request only what your features actually need, and state clearly that inference runs locally in the extension runtime so owners understand where their data is processed.

In a recent development, before the execution loop, it helps to understand how model tool calling works (the basis for any agentic workflow). You pass messages plus a tool schema (name, description, and parameters), and Transformers.js formats the actual prompt from those inputs using the model's chat template. Because chat templates are model-specific, the exact tool-call format depends on the model you use. With Gemma-4-style templates, the model emits a special tool-call token block when it decides to call one.

At generation time, the model can emit output like:.

That is exactly why this project has a normalization layer (webMcp) and a parser (extractToolCalls): model output must be converted into deterministic tool executions.

src/background/agent/webMcp.tsx normalizes extension tools into a model-friendly shape:.

Example tools include get_open_tabs, go_to_tab, open_url, close_tab, find_history, ask_website, and highlight_website_element.

The core design choice here is to separate internal model messages from UI-facing chat messages:.

This keeps user communication clean while preserving a deterministic tool loop in the background.

State placement is another architectural decision that matters a lot in MV3. In this implementation, state is split by lifecycle and access pattern:.

Sources indicate that as described in section 1.2, keeping conversation history in background gives one canonical state across UI updates. This keeps short-lived state in memory, durable settings in extension storage, and heavy retrieval data in a local database.

You do not need a complex build setup, but MV3 does require predictable outputs for each runtime.

The goal is simple: one artifact per Chrome entry point, in the exact place public/manifest.json expects.

The architecture choice that unlocks this whole project is clear separation of concerns: background owns orchestration and model execution, UI surfaces stay thin, and content scripts handle page access.

This project uses a side panel, but the same approach works for other setups:.

The practical rule is simple: decide where state lives (global, tabId, or site-scoped), keep that state and the model inference in background (basically as background services), and let UI/content runtimes act as focused clients.

Latest Update: Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 review: A quiet and compact Wildcat

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Minisforum’s smallest and cheapest mini PC packing Intel's Wildcat Lake silicon is here.
  • Capable enough for home office and media consumption.
  • Only old or lightweight games and emulators are playable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minisforum’s smallest and cheapest mini PC packing Intel's Wildcat Lake silicon is here. It is small, quiet, and easy to stow away, but this machine's performance is really only for light workloads.

Capable enough for home office and media consumption.

Weak performance in creator tasks.

Only old or lightweight games and emulators are playable.

Not a cheap option unless you have spare parts and go barebones.

Single SODIMM and single M.2 slot.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Minisforum’s Intel-based M2 line includes mini PCs with powerful processors such as the Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H (with 16C/16T CPU and B390 graphics), and the Core Ultra 7 356H (16C/16T). But there are more modest systems, too. The M2 Air-304 here is the most affordable option, based around the Intel Core 3 processor 304 with its 5C/5T CPU (1x Cougar Cove P-core and 4x Darkmont LP E-cores) and an iGPU with just a single Xe3 core.

No surprise, the little brother in the pack, both in terms of physical size and computing resources, is the most affordable. It at the moment starts at $263 for a barebones version. However, our test sample with 16GB DDR5-5600, a 500GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro is listed at $559 - direct. That’s an introductory price, and Minisforum’s small text threatens that our configuration will bump up to $699 at some point in the future. Such a rise would put this product offering on very shaky ground, and we see B&H Photo has already raised the price at $729.

Industry observers note that overall, this Mini PC was pleasant to use, though. It ran quietly and only strained in gaming and productivity benchmarks which put it under loads that casual users aren’t going to be running on such a machine.

Sources indicate that the Mini M2 Air looks stylish enough, and feels solid. Looks can be deceiving, though, and the top shell is a silver colored plastic, not a metallic alloy. Sometimes a metal shell can be used to help conduct away heat, but that seems less important with this actively cooled machine with a 15W processor. We note that there are thermal pads connecting the installed RAM and SSD to the bottom of this mini PC, which is metal.

Industry observers note that A VESA mounting bracket is provided in the box if you prefer to hide the tiny device out of sight. It doesn’t have a remote power switch like the MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG we reviewed earlier in the year, though, so you’ll have to consider reachability. A simple LED-lit power button is on the front of the device, alongside a couple of handy ports (more on the ports later). It also has a reset / clear CMOS hole on the front, and a Kensington lock slot on the rear.

Minisforum’s component choices mean this is a particularly small and light mini PC. The official M2 Mini specs state it is 112 x 112 x 37.15mm, which is roughly 4.4 x 4.4 x 1.5-inches. That’s a volume of 0.47 liters. It weighs in at just 440 grams, which is 0.97 pounds.

According to recent reports, the power supply isn’t built-in. There’s a surprisingly bulky 65W power brick in the box, which connects to using a detachable figure-eight cable. However, this mini PC can be powered by USB-C, too, so you could pack a far more compact multipurpose power brick if portability is important.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Intel Core 3 304 (5C/5T) ‘Wildcat Lake,’ up to 4.3 GHz, 15W.

Intel integrated graphics, 1x Xe3 core runs at up to 2.3 GHz, supports up to 3x displays.

16GB in single SODIMM slot which can fit up to a 64GB DDR5-6400 module.

1x M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD slot (up to 2TB), microSD card expansion.

Front: 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2, 3.5mm audio. Rear: 1x USB4 (40Gbps, DP Alt Mode, PD), 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 1x USB 2.0, 2x HDMI 2.0, 2x RJ-45 2.5GbE LAN, DC-IN. Side: microSD card slot.

112 × 112 × 37.15 mm (0.47 L chassis).

Windows 11; barebone model available without OS.

$559.00 limited-time price(16GB RAM, 500GB SSD, Windows 11 Pro).

On the front of the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 there are 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 ports and a 3.5mm audio jack. Turn it to the side and you’ll see the microSD card slot. Then, around the back you have access to 1x USB4 (40Gbps, DP Alt Mode, PD), 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 1x USB 2.0, 2x HDMI 2.0, 2x RJ-45 2.5GbE LAN, and a DC-IN barrel jack.

Sources indicate that some might like to have at least one of the Type-C ports on the front, instead of two Type-As. But for its size the Mini M2 Air packs quite a few ports, including the very capable USB4, two HDMI ports, and two Ethernet ports. Realistically, a machine like this won’t be connected to oodles of wired peripherals, but if you found the port count lacking, USB4 allows for a capable and fast dock.

Wireless connectivity seems adequate, with an M.2 2230 card inside providing Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.4. I had no problems with either during the test period. The wireless card is socketed. It's located under the SSD, making it easy to repair or upgrade down the line.

Accessing the components inside the Minisforum Mini M2 Air is straightforward, but you need to peel off all the four rubber feet to get to four long fastening screws. When they’re removed, just flip off the metal bottom to access the M.2 slots and SODIMM. Be aware there’s some adhesive force holding this metal plate in place, due to the sticky thermal pads on the RAM and storage.

Sources indicate that there’s just a single M.2 2280 storage slot and one SODIMM slot, both populated. That means, there’s no way to upgrade the RAM than swapping the module you already have in place. Our sample came with a 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM, but the system supports up to DDR5-6400. This only non-barebones configuration also came with a 500GB SSD in the M.2 slot.

Intel Arc graphics (Xe-LPG, 8 cores, up to 2.35 GHz).
